text: . Introduction Accurate inpatient blood glucose documentation is essential for safe diabetes management, yet paper-based monitoring systems often record glucose values at clock time rather than during physiologically relevant monitoring periods
title: Improving the Clinical Interpretability of Inpatient Blood Glucose Monitoring Through a Standardized Documentation Chart: A Quality Improvement Study at a Tertiary Public Hospital in the Caribbean.

text: . This quality improvement study evaluated whether implementing a standardized, timing-based diabetes monitoring chart improved the completeness and clinical interpretability of inpatient blood glucose documentation at a tertiary public hospital in the Caribbean. Materials and methods A two-cycle clinical audit was conducted over six months
title: Improving the Clinical Interpretability of Inpatient Blood Glucose Monitoring Through a Standardized Documentation Chart: A Quality Improvement Study at a Tertiary Public Hospital in the Caribbean.

text: . Twenty-five adult medical inpatients with type 2 diabetes mellitus were evaluated before and after implementation of the intervention
title: Improving the Clinical Interpretability of Inpatient Blood Glucose Monitoring Through a Standardized Documentation Chart: A Quality Improvement Study at a Tertiary Public Hospital in the Caribbean.

text: . The intervention consisted of a redesigned paper-based diabetes monitoring chart implemented hospital-wide, which recorded blood glucose measurements during pre-breakfast, pre-lunch, pre-supper, and bedtime monitoring periods, with adjacent documentation of insulin administration and staff education. The primary outcome was the proportion of clinically interpretable diabetes monitoring charts
title: Improving the Clinical Interpretability of Inpatient Blood Glucose Monitoring Through a Standardized Documentation Chart: A Quality Improvement Study at a Tertiary Public Hospital in the Caribbean.

text: . Secondary outcomes included documentation of meal-related blood glucose timing, insulin administration in close proximity to blood glucose measurements, and incomplete diabetes monitoring charts. Results A total of 50 patient records were reviewed. Clinically interpretable documentation increased from 10/25 (40%) at baseline to 23/25 (92%, p < 0.001) following implementation
title: Improving the Clinical Interpretability of Inpatient Blood Glucose Monitoring Through a Standardized Documentation Chart: A Quality Improvement Study at a Tertiary Public Hospital in the Caribbean.

text: . Documentation of meal-related blood glucose timing improved from 9/25 (36%) to 23/25 (92%, p < 0.001), while documentation of insulin administration adjacent to blood glucose measurements increased from 14/25 (56%) to 24/25 (96%, p < 0.001)
title: Improving the Clinical Interpretability of Inpatient Blood Glucose Monitoring Through a Standardized Documentation Chart: A Quality Improvement Study at a Tertiary Public Hospital in the Caribbean.

text: . Overall compliance with predefined documentation standards improved from 11/25 (44%) to 23/25 (92%, p < 0.001), and the number of incomplete diabetes monitoring charts decreased from 8/25 (32%) to 2/25 (8%, p = 0.074)
title: Improving the Clinical Interpretability of Inpatient Blood Glucose Monitoring Through a Standardized Documentation Chart: A Quality Improvement Study at a Tertiary Public Hospital in the Caribbean.

text: . Conclusions Implementation of a standardized timing-based diabetes monitoring chart was associated with marked improvements in the completeness and interpretability of inpatient blood glucose documentation
title: Improving the Clinical Interpretability of Inpatient Blood Glucose Monitoring Through a Standardized Documentation Chart: A Quality Improvement Study at a Tertiary Public Hospital in the Caribbean.

text: . This simple, low-cost quality improvement intervention may enhance inpatient diabetes documentation in hospitals that continue to rely on paper-based medical records and could be adapted for use in other resource-limited healthcare settings.
title: Improving the Clinical Interpretability of Inpatient Blood Glucose Monitoring Through a Standardized Documentation Chart: A Quality Improvement Study at a Tertiary Public Hospital in the Caribbean.

text: Indigenous application of self-management: A concept analysis.. To report an analysis of the concept of self-management in the context of type 2 diabetes, examining how it has been defined, understood, and applied within Indigenous contexts and grounded in Indigenous ways of knowing. Concept analysis
title: Indigenous application of self-management: A concept analysis.
journal: International journal of nursing studies advances

text: . Concept analysis. Keywords and Medical Subject Headings for self-management, type 2 diabetes, and Indigenous Peoples were used to search six databases for articles published in English from January 2002-May 2026
title: Indigenous application of self-management: A concept analysis.
journal: International journal of nursing studies advances

text: . The six steps of Rodgers' evolutionary concept analysis guided the search, with specific attention to how the concept of self-management was defined, applied, and understood in Indigenous contexts
title: Indigenous application of self-management: A concept analysis.
journal: International journal of nursing studies advances

text: . The analysis focused on studies involving Indigenous Peoples living in Canada, the United States, Australia, and New Zealand and examined attributes, antecedents, and consequences of the concept of self-management as applied in Indigenous contexts. After full text screening, a total of 15 articles were included in the final concept analysis
title: Indigenous application of self-management: A concept analysis.
journal: International journal of nursing studies advances

text: . Antecedents of the self-management of type 2 diabetes from an Indigenous perspective included self-determination, cultural continuity, impact of colonization, problem solving skills, and respect for traditions. Attributes were classified into seven categories: physical function, cognitive ability, spirituality, cultural connection, access to care, knowledge regarding diabetes, and social support
title: Indigenous application of self-management: A concept analysis.
journal: International journal of nursing studies advances

text: . Consequences of the self-management of type 2 diabetes among Indigenous Peoples were classified into two categories that included wholistic well-being and cultural resiliency. Findings from this concept analysis highlight that "self-management," as defined in Western biomedical literature, is a relatively recent construct
title: Indigenous application of self-management: A concept analysis.
journal: International journal of nursing studies advances

text: . However, Indigenous Peoples have long engaged in practices of balance, wellness, and collective responsibility for health that align with and expand beyond this concept
title: Indigenous application of self-management: A concept analysis.
journal: International journal of nursing studies advances

text: . Situating type 2 diabetes self-management within Indigenous contexts underscores the importance of Indigenous perspectives of health and well-being while acknowledging the ongoing harmful effects of colonial violence on these practices. Self-management from an Indigenous perspective is complex, with strong socio-historical underpinnings
title: Indigenous application of self-management: A concept analysis.
journal: International journal of nursing studies advances

text: . This concept analysis informs a broad wholistic approach to education when discussing the self-management of type 2 diabetes with Indigenous Peoples. This approach must focus on physical function, cognitive ability, spirituality, cultural connection, access to care, education, and social support
title: Indigenous application of self-management: A concept analysis.
journal: International journal of nursing studies advances

text: . Integrating Indigenous perspectives into self-management approaches can support more culturally safe, relational, and contextually relevant care for individuals living with type 2 diabetes.No Patient or Public Contribution.
title: Indigenous application of self-management: A concept analysis.
journal: International journal of nursing studies advances

text: Nutrition Care and Dietetic Practice in Managing Metabolic and Endocrine Dysfunction in Polyendocrine Metabolic Ovarian Syndrome (PMOS): Implications and Opportunities in the Context of the Name Change of Polycystic Ovarian Syndrome to PMOS.. Polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome (PMOS) affects 8‒13% of women across the lifespan
title: Nutrition Care and Dietetic Practice in Managing Metabolic and Endocrine Dysfunction in Polyendocrine Metabolic Ovarian Syndrome (PMOS): Implications and Opportunities in the Context of the Name Change of Polycystic Ovarian Syndrome to PMOS.

text: . Those with PMOS have reduced quality of life and increased risk of comorbidities, including elevated weight, eating disorders, gestational diabetes, type 2 diabetes, and cardiovascular disease
title: Nutrition Care and Dietetic Practice in Managing Metabolic and Endocrine Dysfunction in Polyendocrine Metabolic Ovarian Syndrome (PMOS): Implications and Opportunities in the Context of the Name Change of Polycystic Ovarian Syndrome to PMOS.

text: . PMOS is a major population in clinical dietetic practice, and dietary intervention is the first-line approach recommended to target metabolic risk in the international evidence-based guidelines for assessment and management of polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS)
title: Nutrition Care and Dietetic Practice in Managing Metabolic and Endocrine Dysfunction in Polyendocrine Metabolic Ovarian Syndrome (PMOS): Implications and Opportunities in the Context of the Name Change of Polycystic Ovarian Syndrome to PMOS.

text: . The past name, PCOS, was ovarian-centric and did not accurately reflect the pathophysiology, endocrine, or metabolic dysfunction of the syndrome
title: Nutrition Care and Dietetic Practice in Managing Metabolic and Endocrine Dysfunction in Polyendocrine Metabolic Ovarian Syndrome (PMOS): Implications and Opportunities in the Context of the Name Change of Polycystic Ovarian Syndrome to PMOS.

text: . The new name, PMOS, has been determined by a rigorous global consensus process including 56 organizations, >14,000 survey responses, and consultation with experts and patients in workshops that identified the need for accurate medical representation of the syndrome and a stigma-reducing name
title: Nutrition Care and Dietetic Practice in Managing Metabolic and Endocrine Dysfunction in Polyendocrine Metabolic Ovarian Syndrome (PMOS): Implications and Opportunities in the Context of the Name Change of Polycystic Ovarian Syndrome to PMOS.

text: . Dietitians encounter patients with PMOS with increased cardiometabolic risk who also experience high rates of elevated weight, weight stigma, and eating disorders. Nutrition care of patients with PMOS often involves managing these conditions, use of anti-obesity and diabetes medications, conferring with prescribing clinicians, and navigating patient goals and preferences
title: Nutrition Care and Dietetic Practice in Managing Metabolic and Endocrine Dysfunction in Polyendocrine Metabolic Ovarian Syndrome (PMOS): Implications and Opportunities in the Context of the Name Change of Polycystic Ovarian Syndrome to PMOS.

text: . Improved recognition of the metabolic risks can strengthen alignment with dietary management approaches and referral to nutrition care services as part of the multidisciplinary care needed in those with PMOS. Dietitians can play a key role in managing nutritional misinformation, supporting patient health literacy and nutritional self-management
title: Nutrition Care and Dietetic Practice in Managing Metabolic and Endocrine Dysfunction in Polyendocrine Metabolic Ovarian Syndrome (PMOS): Implications and Opportunities in the Context of the Name Change of Polycystic Ovarian Syndrome to PMOS.

text: . The new name can contribute to expanded opportunities for nutritional research that targets endocrine and metabolic outcomes to improve the clinical care, health, and well-being of those living with PMOS.
title: Nutrition Care and Dietetic Practice in Managing Metabolic and Endocrine Dysfunction in Polyendocrine Metabolic Ovarian Syndrome (PMOS): Implications and Opportunities in the Context of the Name Change of Polycystic Ovarian Syndrome to PMOS.

text: From Gila Monster Venom to Dermatology: The History of GLP-1 Receptor Agonists.. Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RAs) have evolved from novel therapies for type 2 diabetes mellitus into widely used treatments for obesity and metabolic disease
title: From Gila Monster Venom to Dermatology: The History of GLP-1 Receptor Agonists.

text: . Their origins can be traced to the Gila monster (Heloderma suspectum), a venomous lizard native to the deserts of the southwestern United States and northwestern Mexico. The discovery of exendin-4, a peptide isolated from the venom of the Gila monster, led to the subsequent development of longer acting GLP-1RAs
title: From Gila Monster Venom to Dermatology: The History of GLP-1 Receptor Agonists.

text: . Long before its contribution to modern medicine would be recognized, the Gila monster was revered in Navajo culture and folklore. We have examined the historic development of GLP-1 RAs, from the natural history and cultural significance of the Gila monster to the discovery of exendin-4 and the subsequent development of modern therapeutics
title: From Gila Monster Venom to Dermatology: The History of GLP-1 Receptor Agonists.

text: . We describe the scientific advances that led to the translation of a venom-derived peptide into a major therapeutic class, including the development of exenatide, liraglutide and semaglutide. The history of GLP-1 receptor agonists demonstrates how observations in nature can lead to major therapeutic advances
title: From Gila Monster Venom to Dermatology: The History of GLP-1 Receptor Agonists.

text: . What began with a view of a venomous desert lizard has evolved into one of the most important therapeutic classes in modern metabolic medicine, with expanding therapeutic applications in dermatology. The Gila monster (Heloderma suspectum) is a venomous lizard native to the deserts of the southwestern United States and northwestern Mexico
title: From Gila Monster Venom to Dermatology: The History of GLP-1 Receptor Agonists.

text: . Long revered in indigenous cultural traditions, the Gila monster made an unexpected contribution to modern medicine. The discovery of exendin-4, a peptide within its venom, ultimately led to the development of glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RAs), representing one of the most significant therapeutic advances in modern metabolic medicine
title: From Gila Monster Venom to Dermatology: The History of GLP-1 Receptor Agonists.

text: . GLP-1RAs are synthetic polypeptides that mimic the actions of the endogenous incretin hormone glucagon-like peptide-1. Initially developed for the treatment of type 2 diabetes mellitus, they have transformed obesity management and are now among the most widely prescribed therapies worldwide
title: From Gila Monster Venom to Dermatology: The History of GLP-1 Receptor Agonists.

text: . As recognition of obesity has emerged as a major global public health challenge, GLP-1RAs have provided an effective pharmacologic approach to weight management. According to the World Health Organization, more than 1 billion people worldwide have been living with obesity as of 2022 [1]
title: From Gila Monster Venom to Dermatology: The History of GLP-1 Receptor Agonists.

text: . The success of GLP-1RAs can be traced to the discovery of exendin-4, a peptide isolated from Gila monster venom that shares key biologic properties with human GLP-1 while demonstrating greater resistance to enzymatic degradation
title: From Gila Monster Venom to Dermatology: The History of GLP-1 Receptor Agonists.

text: . Emerging evidence suggests that GLP-1RAs may influence inflammatory skin disease through a combination of weight reduction, improvements in metabolic health, and modulation of inflammatory and immune pathways [2]. This has generated increasing interest in the potential applications of GLP-1RAs within dermatology
title: From Gila Monster Venom to Dermatology: The History of GLP-1 Receptor Agonists.

text: . In this review, we have examined the cultural significance and physiologic adaptations of the Gila monster, the discovery of exendin-4 and the subsequent development of GLP-1 RAs from venom-derived peptide to an expanding modern therapeutic class
title: From Gila Monster Venom to Dermatology: The History of GLP-1 Receptor Agonists.

text: . We have explored how observations from a venomous desert lizard has translated into one of the most important therapeutic advances in metabolic medicine with evolving therapeutic applications in dermatology.
title: From Gila Monster Venom to Dermatology: The History of GLP-1 Receptor Agonists.

text: Minimally invasive treatment of recurrent varicose veins with thrombotic complications using EVLA: A case report.. We present a clinical case of a 59-year-old male who complained of varicose veins and a burning sensation in the right lower limb
title: Minimally invasive treatment of recurrent varicose veins with thrombotic complications using EVLA: A case report.

text: . His medical history included bilateral great saphenous vein (GSV) removal (2003), type 2 diabetes mellitus, stage 4 chronic kidney disease, gout, and arterial hypertension. Duplex ultrasound revealed varicothrombophlebitis of the small saphenous vein (SSV) and a floating thrombus in the popliteal vein
title: Minimally invasive treatment of recurrent varicose veins with thrombotic complications using EVLA: A case report.

text: . Initial treatment consisted of oral anticoagulation with rivaroxaban, followed by EVLA of the SSV and ultrasound-guided sclerotherapy of tributaries. After anticoagulant therapy, partial recanalization of the SSV and thrombus lysis in the popliteal vein were observed. EVLA of the SSV was performed without complications. Anticoagulant therapy was continued in coordination with a hematologist
title: Minimally invasive treatment of recurrent varicose veins with thrombotic complications using EVLA: A case report.

text: . At 6-month follow-up, duplex ultrasound showed the SSV as a fibrotic cord (diameter 3-4 mm), with regression of symptoms of chronic venous insufficiency. Despite the patient's high-risk profile, individualized management and careful monitoring allowed for the successful performance of a minimally invasive procedure
title: Minimally invasive treatment of recurrent varicose veins with thrombotic complications using EVLA: A case report.

text: . In selected high-risk patients with recurrent varicose disease complicated by thrombosis, EVLA may be considered following appropriate anticoagulant preparation. This case highlights the potential feasibility of an individualized and staged treatment approach in complex clinical settings.
title: Minimally invasive treatment of recurrent varicose veins with thrombotic complications using EVLA: A case report.

text: From Alert to Action: Electronic Practice Advisory Improves DSMES Referrals Over 18 Months.. Engagement in diabetes self-management education and support (DSMES) is suboptimal among people with type 2 diabetes (T2D). The PROMPT study examined whether referral rates to DSMES increased through a best practice advisory (BPA) deployed during clinic visits via the electronic health record
title: From Alert to Action: Electronic Practice Advisory Improves DSMES Referrals Over 18 Months.

text: . In this cluster-randomized controlled trial in central North Carolina, we created a BPA within the electronic health record that deployed when eligible patients with T2D attended primary care visits. The BPA was active in four primary care practices over 18 months, with two control practices
title: From Alert to Action: Electronic Practice Advisory Improves DSMES Referrals Over 18 Months.

text: . After 12 months, standing orders were added so the BPA would additionally deploy for nurses or medical assistants before patients saw their clinician. We analyzed data using multilevel logistic regression modeling with patient data nested within clinics, using binary logit functions and maximum likelihood estimation to estimate the odds of DSMES referrals
title: From Alert to Action: Electronic Practice Advisory Improves DSMES Referrals Over 18 Months.

text: . At 12 months, the BPA intervention achieved a 12.9% DSMES referral rate compared with 1.2% in control clinics (P < 0.001). At 18 months, the referral rate remained higher in the intervention clinics (13.7%) than in controls (1.6%; P < 0.001)
title: From Alert to Action: Electronic Practice Advisory Improves DSMES Referrals Over 18 Months.

text: . After adjusting for patient and clinic characteristics, the odds of referral in BPA-exposed clinics were significantly greater than in control clinics at both time points: odds ratio (OR) 10.55 (95% CI 4.65-23.94) at 12 months and OR 9.44 (95% CI 4.91-18.17) at 18 months after implementation of standing orders
title: From Alert to Action: Electronic Practice Advisory Improves DSMES Referrals Over 18 Months.

text: . Integrating BPA prompts into the electronic health record boosts DSMES referral rates, and adding standing orders helps sustain these gains.
title: From Alert to Action: Electronic Practice Advisory Improves DSMES Referrals Over 18 Months.

text: Characterizing Continuous Glucose Monitoring Prescription Patterns Between 2020 and 2024: A Retrospective Study at a Single Primary Care Facility in the United States.. Examine the factors associated with continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) device prescriptions in a primary care facility
title: Characterizing Continuous Glucose Monitoring Prescription Patterns Between 2020 and 2024: A Retrospective Study at a Single Primary Care Facility in the United States.

text: . We conducted a retrospective study of 1476 patients with Type 1 and Type 2 diabetes receiving care at a single primary care facility between 2020 and 2024. We examined the associations between receiving a CGM prescription and demographic characteristics, health factors, de-identified physician information, and insurance status. We conducted univariate analysis using chi-square tests
title: Characterizing Continuous Glucose Monitoring Prescription Patterns Between 2020 and 2024: A Retrospective Study at a Single Primary Care Facility in the United States.

text: . Multivariate logistic regression models accounted for multiple factors predicting receiving a CGM prescription. The average CGM prescription rate per physician was less than 4%. Various factors were significantly associated with receiving a CGM prescription
title: Characterizing Continuous Glucose Monitoring Prescription Patterns Between 2020 and 2024: A Retrospective Study at a Single Primary Care Facility in the United States.

text: . Notably, younger patients on insulin, with Type 1 diabetes, and higher glycated hemoglobin (HbA1C) values were more likely to be prescribed a CGM device. Patients with nutritional and metabolic diseases or abnormal lab values were less likely to receive a CGM prescription
title: Characterizing Continuous Glucose Monitoring Prescription Patterns Between 2020 and 2024: A Retrospective Study at a Single Primary Care Facility in the United States.

text: . Our findings are similar to those of other CGM studies, which show that CGM prescriptions are significantly higher among patients who are younger and who have Type 1 diabetes. There is a need for future studies that aim to better understand CGM prescribing decision-making among PCPs to inform the development of targeted interventions to improve CGM prescribing rates for all eligible patients.
title: Characterizing Continuous Glucose Monitoring Prescription Patterns Between 2020 and 2024: A Retrospective Study at a Single Primary Care Facility in the United States.

text: Spironolactone-Induced Bilateral Gynecomastia in a Patient With Comorbid Conditions.. Gynecomastia is a benign proliferation of male breast glandular tissue caused by an imbalance between estrogen and androgen activity
title: Spironolactone-Induced Bilateral Gynecomastia in a Patient With Comorbid Conditions.

text: . Spironolactone, a potassium-sparing diuretic commonly prescribed for edema and ascites in chronic liver disease, is a recognized cause of drug-induced gynecomastia because of its antiandrogenic effects. We report the case of a man in his 50s with chronic liver disease and type 2 diabetes mellitus who presented with bilateral breast swelling and mild tenderness of one month's duration
title: Spironolactone-Induced Bilateral Gynecomastia in a Patient With Comorbid Conditions.

text: . Clinical examination revealed bilateral soft glandular enlargement without nipple discharge, a hard mass, or axillary lymphadenopathy. Breast ultrasonography demonstrated diffuse fibroglandular proliferation with subareolar thickening consistent with bilateral gynecomastia
title: Spironolactone-Induced Bilateral Gynecomastia in a Patient With Comorbid Conditions.

text: . Laboratory investigations showed mildly reduced serum testosterone with relative estrogen predominance, while prolactin, luteinizing hormone, follicle-stimulating hormone, and thyroid function tests were within normal limits
title: Spironolactone-Induced Bilateral Gynecomastia in a Patient With Comorbid Conditions.

text: . Chronic liver disease likely contributed to hormonal imbalance through impaired estrogen metabolism and altered sex hormone regulation, thereby increasing susceptibility to spironolactone-induced gynecomastia. Spironolactone therapy was discontinued, and conservative management with clinical monitoring was advised. The patient showed gradual symptomatic improvement during follow-up
title: Spironolactone-Induced Bilateral Gynecomastia in a Patient With Comorbid Conditions.

text: . This case highlights the importance of recognizing medication-induced endocrine adverse effects, particularly in patients with chronic systemic illnesses such as hepatic dysfunction.
title: Spironolactone-Induced Bilateral Gynecomastia in a Patient With Comorbid Conditions.

text: Incremental effects of SGLT2 inhibitors, GLP-1 receptor agonists, and pioglitazone in type 2 diabetes and MASLD across Asian study settings: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
title: Incremental effects of SGLT2 inhibitors, GLP-1 receptor agonists, and pioglitazone in type 2 diabetes and MASLD across Asian study settings: a systematic review and meta-analysis.

text: . We evaluated the incremental hepatic and metabolic effects of adding sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 (SGLT2) inhibitors, glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RAs), or pioglitazone to comparable background glucose-lowering therapy in Asian adults with type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) and metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD)
title: Incremental effects of SGLT2 inhibitors, GLP-1 receptor agonists, and pioglitazone in type 2 diabetes and MASLD across Asian study settings: a systematic review and meta-analysis.

text: . We systematically searched PubMed, Embase, the Cochrane Library, and Web of Science through 30 June 2026. Two reviewers independently screened studies, extracted data, and assessed risk of bias
title: Incremental effects of SGLT2 inhibitors, GLP-1 receptor agonists, and pioglitazone in type 2 diabetes and MASLD across Asian study settings: a systematic review and meta-analysis.

text: . Eligible trials evaluated the addition of a study drug to background glucose-lowering management that was comparable between randomized groups and either remained stable or followed a prespecified adjustment protocol. Changes from baseline in alanine aminotransferase (ALT) and glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c) were coprimary outcomes
title: Incremental effects of SGLT2 inhibitors, GLP-1 receptor agonists, and pioglitazone in type 2 diabetes and MASLD across Asian study settings: a systematic review and meta-analysis.

text: . Secondary outcomes included aspartate aminotransferase, gamma-glutamyl transferase, magnetic resonance imaging-proton density fat fraction, liver stiffness, fibrosis-4 index, fasting plasma glucose, lipid parameters, body mass index, serum adiponectin, and systolic blood pressure
title: Incremental effects of SGLT2 inhibitors, GLP-1 receptor agonists, and pioglitazone in type 2 diabetes and MASLD across Asian study settings: a systematic review and meta-analysis.

text: . Random-effects pairwise meta-analyses were performed, and GRADE certainty was assessed for the two coprimary outcomes. Safety outcomes were synthesized narratively because reporting was heterogeneous and frequently incomplete. We included eleven randomized trials: 692 participants were randomized into eligible comparisons, of which 642 participated in the coprimary efficacy analyses
title: Incremental effects of SGLT2 inhibitors, GLP-1 receptor agonists, and pioglitazone in type 2 diabetes and MASLD across Asian study settings: a systematic review and meta-analysis.

text: . Moderate certainty was found for a reduction in ALT with the addition of an SGLT2 inhibitor compared with background therapy alone (mean difference [MD], - 7.56 U/L; 95% confidence interval [CI], - 11.24 to - 3.88); however, there was little or no clinically important further benefit observed for HbA1c (MD, - 0.09%; 95% CI, - 0.27 to 0.08; moderate certainty)
title: Incremental effects of SGLT2 inhibitors, GLP-1 receptor agonists, and pioglitazone in type 2 diabetes and MASLD across Asian study settings: a systematic review and meta-analysis.

text: . Modest reductions in ALT were suggested by moderate certainty for GLP-1RAs (MD, - 6.71 U/L; 95% CI, - 11.53 to - 1.89) while low certainty indicated an HbA1c reduction (MD, - 0.48%; 95% CI, - 0.83 to - 0.14). Secondary exploratory findings favoring add-on therapy existed, although they are unadjusted for multiplicity. The comparative safety could not be assessed reliably
title: Incremental effects of SGLT2 inhibitors, GLP-1 receptor agonists, and pioglitazone in type 2 diabetes and MASLD across Asian study settings: a systematic review and meta-analysis.

text: . In short-term randomized trials conducted in Asian study settings, adding SGLT2 inhibitors or GLP-1RAs may improve selected hepatic and metabolic surrogate outcomes. The available evidence does not support a treatment-class ranking, and the durability and clinical significance of these changes remain uncertain because follow-up was short and several comparisons were based on sparse evidence
title: Incremental effects of SGLT2 inhibitors, GLP-1 receptor agonists, and pioglitazone in type 2 diabetes and MASLD across Asian study settings: a systematic review and meta-analysis.

text: . Comparative safety also remains uncertain because adverse-event reporting was heterogeneous and incomplete. https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/, identifier CRD420251231137.
title: Incremental effects of SGLT2 inhibitors, GLP-1 receptor agonists, and pioglitazone in type 2 diabetes and MASLD across Asian study settings: a systematic review and meta-analysis.

text: Enhancing Alzheimer's disease diagnosis in primary care through targeted screening of people at risk of developing dementia - study design and feasibility assessment of the PREDEM primary care study.. Timely detection of cognitive impairment due to Alzheimer's disease (AD) is increasingly important as disease modifying therapies become available
title: Enhancing Alzheimer's disease diagnosis in primary care through targeted screening of people at risk of developing dementia - study design and feasibility assessment of the PREDEM primary care study.

text: . Current diagnostic pathways in primary health care (PHC) rely mainly on clinical assessment and brief cognitive screening tools, which lack sensitivity for early impairment. Blood-based biomarkers (BBMs) show promising diagnostic potential in research settings
title: Enhancing Alzheimer's disease diagnosis in primary care through targeted screening of people at risk of developing dementia - study design and feasibility assessment of the PREDEM primary care study.

text: . Targeted screening of individuals with cognitive symptoms and dementia risk factors using sensitive cognitive tests and reliable biomarkers may improve early AD detection in PHC. The PREDEM primary care study evaluates a targeted screening strategy combining a multidomain digital cognitive test battery and BBMs in individuals having elevated risk of dementia
title: Enhancing Alzheimer's disease diagnosis in primary care through targeted screening of people at risk of developing dementia - study design and feasibility assessment of the PREDEM primary care study.

text: . This pilot study assessed the feasibility of recruitment, digital cognitive testing, biomarker sampling, and data collection. This descriptive pilot study was conducted at two PHC centres in Stockholm (April-October 2024). Eligible individuals were aged ≥ 65 years with hypertension or type 2 diabetes and self-reported memory complaints
title: Enhancing Alzheimer's disease diagnosis in primary care through targeted screening of people at risk of developing dementia - study design and feasibility assessment of the PREDEM primary care study.

text: . Participants completed a screening question, followed by a demographic questionnaire, a multidomain digital cognitive test battery (Mindmore), MMSE, and blood sampling for four BBMs (GFAP, NF‑L, total tau, pTau217). Feasibility metrics included recruitment yield, test completion rates, participant characteristics, cognitive performance, and biomarker distributions
title: Enhancing Alzheimer's disease diagnosis in primary care through targeted screening of people at risk of developing dementia - study design and feasibility assessment of the PREDEM primary care study.

text: . Of 548 identified individuals, 307 were invited and 40 were enrolled (13% participation). Among those enrolled, 37 completed all parts of the study. Digital home-based testing proved challenging: although 22 participants initially opted for home testing, only six completed it independently, and most required clinic-based support
title: Enhancing Alzheimer's disease diagnosis in primary care through targeted screening of people at risk of developing dementia - study design and feasibility assessment of the PREDEM primary care study.

text: . Across cognitive tests, approximately one-third of participants scored below 1 standard deviation of normative performance, indicating detectable cognitive impairment. Non-native Swedish speakers (32%) showed significantly lower performance on verbally mediated tasks
title: Enhancing Alzheimer's disease diagnosis in primary care through targeted screening of people at risk of developing dementia - study design and feasibility assessment of the PREDEM primary care study.

text: . Established cut-off values for pTau217 reflecting amyloid pathology showed pathological levels in 10-23% of participants depending on single or double cut-offs. This pilot study demonstrates the feasibility of the PREDEM primary care study design and data collection procedures
title: Enhancing Alzheimer's disease diagnosis in primary care through targeted screening of people at risk of developing dementia - study design and feasibility assessment of the PREDEM primary care study.

text: . Targeted recruitment of older adults with cardiometabolic risk factors was able to identify a population relevant to the study aims. Key protocol refinements include removing the requirement for subjective memory complaints, conducting all cognitive testing at PHC, and optimization of cognitive test battery.
title: Enhancing Alzheimer's disease diagnosis in primary care through targeted screening of people at risk of developing dementia - study design and feasibility assessment of the PREDEM primary care study.

text: Nurse-led behavioural support for lifestyle self-management in adults with type 2 diabetes mellitus: an integrative review.. Type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) requires sustained self-management across diet, physical activity, body weight, glucose monitoring, and medication-taking behaviours
title: Nurse-led behavioural support for lifestyle self-management in adults with type 2 diabetes mellitus: an integrative review.

text: . Although lifestyle recommendations are central to diabetes care, patients often need professional support to translate advice into feasible, culturally acceptable, and safe daily routines. To synthesize evidence on lifestyle interventions and nurse-led behavioural support for adults with T2DM, and to clarify implications for nursing self-management support and service delivery
title: Nurse-led behavioural support for lifestyle self-management in adults with type 2 diabetes mellitus: an integrative review.

text: . An integrative review with narrative synthesis was conducted. We searched Embase, the Cochrane Library, Scopus, Web of Science, WanFang Data, VIP, PubMed, and CINAHL for literature published between 2006 and 2026
title: Nurse-led behavioural support for lifestyle self-management in adults with type 2 diabetes mellitus: an integrative review.

text: . To strengthen currency and nursing relevance, we added high-relevance, peer-reviewed studies on nurse-led education, behavioural coaching, medication adherence, technology-enabled support, and self-management. Twenty articles were included, comprising randomized and quasi-experimental studies, systematic reviews and meta-analyses, narrative reviews, position statements, and analytic studies
title: Nurse-led behavioural support for lifestyle self-management in adults with type 2 diabetes mellitus: an integrative review.

text: . Data were summarized using inductive content analysis and appraised narratively for methodological clarity, relevance, and nursing implications; no design-specific formal risk-of-bias assessment, GRADE assessment, or quantitative synthesis was undertaken
title: Nurse-led behavioural support for lifestyle self-management in adults with type 2 diabetes mellitus: an integrative review.

text: . Four interrelated themes were identified: physical activity and dietary habits; weight management and obesity control; structured patient education, behavioural coaching and empowerment; and medication-related support, glucose-monitoring guidance and technology-enabled follow-up. Lifestyle interventions provided the behavioural foundation for T2DM management
title: Nurse-led behavioural support for lifestyle self-management in adults with type 2 diabetes mellitus: an integrative review.

text: . Nurse-led support may strengthen implementation by helping patients set realistic goals, interpret glucose data, address medication concerns, adapt recommendations to cultural and family routines, and maintain follow-up contact. This integrative synthesis suggests that structured lifestyle interventions and nurse-led behavioural support may be useful complementary components of T2DM care
title: Nurse-led behavioural support for lifestyle self-management in adults with type 2 diabetes mellitus: an integrative review.

text: . Nurses may help translate lifestyle recommendations into feasible self-management routines, but the review does not establish comparative effectiveness or superiority over other delivery models. Findings should therefore inform practice-oriented nursing support rather than be interpreted as a graded clinical recommendation.
title: Nurse-led behavioural support for lifestyle self-management in adults with type 2 diabetes mellitus: an integrative review.

text: Behavior change techniques to improve treatment adherence in type 2 diabetes: A systematic review.. Cognitive-behavioral interventions have shown positive results in type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) self-management; however, the lack of detailed descriptions of these interventions makes their replication difficult
title: Behavior change techniques to improve treatment adherence in type 2 diabetes: A systematic review.

text: . This study aims to identify behavioral change techniques (BCT) for improving adherence to medication, diet, and exercise in adults with T2DM. We conducted a systematic search in June 2024 across PubMed, Cochrane, Web of Science, PsycINFO, and CINAHL to identify studies published since 2013 that examined BCTs aimed at improving treatment adherence in adults with T2DM
title: Behavior change techniques to improve treatment adherence in type 2 diabetes: A systematic review.

text: . A total of 6 articles - including randomized controlled trials, a scoping review, and systematic reviews - were included, addressing adherence to medication, diet, and exercise
title: Behavior change techniques to improve treatment adherence in type 2 diabetes: A systematic review.

text: . BCTs associated with improved adherence and reported across multiple studies included action planning (1.4), social support (unspecified) (3.1), social support (practical) (3.2), instruction on how to perform a behavior (4.1), information about health consequences (5.1), prompts and cues (7.1), and credible source (9.1)
title: Behavior change techniques to improve treatment adherence in type 2 diabetes: A systematic review.

text: . The findings highlight the importance of clearly structured intervention descriptions and the use of robust theoretical frameworks. Future interventions should incorporate components targeting patient education, skill development, and support networks to enhance adherence to dietary recommendations, physical activity, and pharmacological treatment.
title: Behavior change techniques to improve treatment adherence in type 2 diabetes: A systematic review.

text: Temporal patterns of tuberculosis-associated hyperglycaemia and its effect on treatment outcomes in individuals not previously diabetic: A prospective cohort study.. Active tuberculosis (TB) infection can induce hyperglycaemia and insulin resistance, increasing the risk of type 2 diabetes mellitus and worsening TB disease severity
title: Temporal patterns of tuberculosis-associated hyperglycaemia and its effect on treatment outcomes in individuals not previously diabetic: A prospective cohort study.

text: . However, data on the dynamics of TB-associated hyperglycaemia and its effect on TB treatment outcomes among individuals not previously diabetic remain limited, particularly in high TB-burden settings
title: Temporal patterns of tuberculosis-associated hyperglycaemia and its effect on treatment outcomes in individuals not previously diabetic: A prospective cohort study.

text: . In this study, we aimed to investigate the prevalence and temporal patterns of TB-associated hyperglycaemia and its impact on disease presentation and TB treatment outcomes among a cohort of individuals not previously diabetic
title: Temporal patterns of tuberculosis-associated hyperglycaemia and its effect on treatment outcomes in individuals not previously diabetic: A prospective cohort study.

text: . This was a five-month longitudinal prospective cohort study conducted at two urban specialized TB healthcare facilities in Kenya among adults aged >18 years with bacteriologically confirmed pulmonary TB (PTB). Known diabetes mellitus (DM) or prediabetic individuals were excluded during enrolment
title: Temporal patterns of tuberculosis-associated hyperglycaemia and its effect on treatment outcomes in individuals not previously diabetic: A prospective cohort study.

text: . Glycaemic status was assessed at baseline and months two and five using glycated haemoglobin (HbA1c) according to the American Diabetes Association guideline. Hyperglycaemia was defined as HbA1c ≥5.7% and categorized as normoglycaemia, persistent, transient, or incident hyperglycaemia based on longitudinal measurements
title: Temporal patterns of tuberculosis-associated hyperglycaemia and its effect on treatment outcomes in individuals not previously diabetic: A prospective cohort study.

text: . Socio-demographic and clinical data were collected using a structured questionnaire and analysed using SPSS version 26.0 and GraphPad Prism version 9.0. Longitudinal trends in HbA1c levels and the association of hyperglycaemia with DM-related symptoms, as well as TB treatment outcomes, were assessed using the Friedman test and the Generalized Estimating Equations (GEE), respectively
title: Temporal patterns of tuberculosis-associated hyperglycaemia and its effect on treatment outcomes in individuals not previously diabetic: A prospective cohort study.

text: . We enrolled and followed 87 individuals newly diagnosed with PTB. Of these, 66 were tested for hyperglycaemia in month two after 7 died and 14 were lost to follow-up/transferred out (LTFU/TO), and 70 in month 5, after an additional death, 7 re-engagements, and 2 LTFU/TO were reported
title: Temporal patterns of tuberculosis-associated hyperglycaemia and its effect on treatment outcomes in individuals not previously diabetic: A prospective cohort study.

text: . At enrolment, the cohort was predominantly male (76%), not married (53%), and HIV-negative (84%), with a median age of 37 years (IQR 29-44). Prevalence of hyperglycaemia at baseline was 75% (95% Confidence Interval [CI] 65-83), with 45% of the individuals presenting as prediabetic and 30% as diabetic
title: Temporal patterns of tuberculosis-associated hyperglycaemia and its effect on treatment outcomes in individuals not previously diabetic: A prospective cohort study.

text: . At the month-two and month-five time points, the proportion of participants with prediabetes (pre-DM) increased from 24% (16/66) to 30% (21/70), while the prevalence of DM declined from 21% (14/66) to 9% (6/70). Across the time points, HbA1c levels varied significantly (p < 0.001)
title: Temporal patterns of tuberculosis-associated hyperglycaemia and its effect on treatment outcomes in individuals not previously diabetic: A prospective cohort study.

text: . In GEE analysis, hyperglycaemic participants were more likely to experience classic symptoms of DM such as frequent micturition (adjusted Relative Risk [aRR] 1.76, 95% CI 1.12-2.77), increased thirst (aRR 2.37, 95% CI 1.38-4.05), unintentional weight loss (aRR 1.84, 95% CI 1.24-2.75), and blurred vision (aRR 1.95, 95% CI 1.20-3.18)
title: Temporal patterns of tuberculosis-associated hyperglycaemia and its effect on treatment outcomes in individuals not previously diabetic: A prospective cohort study.

text: . After adjusting for age, BMI, HIV, alcohol use, and smoking, hyperglycaemia was independently associated with an increased risk of sputum positivity (aRR 4.22, 95% CI 2.09-8.52). Glycaemic variability was significantly associated with unfavourable TB treatment outcomes (p < 0.001)
title: Temporal patterns of tuberculosis-associated hyperglycaemia and its effect on treatment outcomes in individuals not previously diabetic: A prospective cohort study.

text: . New-onset hyperglycaemia was highly prevalent in adults newly diagnosed with TB and persisted through the fifth month of TB treatment. Hyperglycaemia was associated with classic diabetic symptoms and persisting sputum positivity, highlighting the need to integrate glycaemic monitoring and management into routine TB follow-up care.
title: Temporal patterns of tuberculosis-associated hyperglycaemia and its effect on treatment outcomes in individuals not previously diabetic: A prospective cohort study.

text: Understanding type 2 diabetes self-management in the Marshall Islands: A mixed-methods exploration of sociocultural and structural barriers.. Type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) poses a critical public health challenge in the Republic of the Marshall Islands, where prevalence rates are among the highest globally
title: Understanding type 2 diabetes self-management in the Marshall Islands: A mixed-methods exploration of sociocultural and structural barriers.

text: . Despite the central role of self-management in diabetes care, adherence and utilization of health services remain inadequate and are major contributors to diabetes-related morbidity and mortality. We aimed to identify factors influencing self-management and to explore the sociocultural context shaping these behaviors using an explanatory sequential mixed methods approach
title: Understanding type 2 diabetes self-management in the Marshall Islands: A mixed-methods exploration of sociocultural and structural barriers.

text: . From March to May 2023, we surveyed 123 randomly selected T2DM outpatients aged 18 years and older in Majuro Atoll. We assessed self-management practices, illness perception, diabetes knowledge, clinical characteristics, and sociodemographic factors, and used regression analysis to identify key predictors of self-management
title: Understanding type 2 diabetes self-management in the Marshall Islands: A mixed-methods exploration of sociocultural and structural barriers.

text: . Subsequently, semi-structured interviews with ten patients and three healthcare providers were conducted and analyzed thematically. Findings revealed that 76% of participants demonstrated inadequate self-management. Despite 90% recognizing diet as a causative factor, dietary control scored lowest among self-management domains, highlighting a disconnect between awareness and action
title: Understanding type 2 diabetes self-management in the Marshall Islands: A mixed-methods exploration of sociocultural and structural barriers.

text: . A higher perceived threat of illness was associated with poorer self-management, suggesting that fear may discourage rather than encourage coping action. While attending diabetes education classes was positively associated, diabetes knowledge level was not a significant predictor
title: Understanding type 2 diabetes self-management in the Marshall Islands: A mixed-methods exploration of sociocultural and structural barriers.

text: . Three key themes emerged as barriers to self-management that lie beyond individual control: i.Dysfunctional healthcare service delivery, ii. Diabetes fatalism, and iii. Food desert
title: Understanding type 2 diabetes self-management in the Marshall Islands: A mixed-methods exploration of sociocultural and structural barriers.

text: . Diabetes fatalism, and iii. Food desert. This study highlights the need for culturally tailored health education, psychological support to counter diabetes fatalism along with strengthening health systems to better respond to patient needs, and policies to improve food security, which are critical to improving diabetes outcomes in this high-risk population.

text: Consensus-based clinical and research recommendations for use of glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists in the context of eating disorders: a modified Delphi study.. title: Consensus-based clinical and research recommendations for use of glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists in the context of eating disorders: a modified Delphi study.

text: . However, the appetite-suppressing and weight-loss effects of GLP-1RAs raise concerns about misuse and potential exacerbation or emergence of eating disorders (EDs). Evidence remains limited and inconsistent, requiring structured, expert-informed guidance
title: Consensus-based clinical and research recommendations for use of glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists in the context of eating disorders: a modified Delphi study.
journal: World psychiatry : official journal of the World Psychiatric Association (WPA)

text: . Using a modified three-round Delphi method, a multidisciplinary panel of experts in diabetes, obesity and/or EDs, and individuals with lived experience of an ED and/or GLP-1RA use (N=45) achieved ≥70% consensus on recommendations (average consensus: 91.7%)
title: Consensus-based clinical and research recommendations for use of glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists in the context of eating disorders: a modified Delphi study.
journal: World psychiatry : official journal of the World Psychiatric Association (WPA)

text: . Clinical recommendations include: a) the implementation of screening for current and historical ED before initiating GLP-1RAs, using a brief psychometrically validated instrument; b) routine monitoring of ED symptoms with intensity stratified by risk level; c) the development of standardized educational materials for patients and providers; and d) offering concurrent evidence-based psychotherapy
title: Consensus-based clinical and research recommendations for use of glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists in the context of eating disorders: a modified Delphi study.

These medications should generally be avoided in individuals with active EDs, particularly anorexia nervosa, atypical anorexia nervosa, and bulimia nervosa with marked dietary restraint and/or significant weight suppression. text: outcomes of GLP-1RAs in individuals with binge eating disorder
title: Consensus-based clinical and research recommendations for use of glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists in the context of eating disorders: a modified Delphi study.
journal: World psychiatry : official journal of the World Psychiatric Association (WPA)

text: Rhino-Orbital-Cerebral Mucormycosis With Intracranial Extension in a Patient With Diabetic Ketoacidosis.. Rhino-orbital-cerebral mucormycosis (ROCM) is a rare but highly aggressive fungal infection that predominantly affects immunocompromised individuals, with diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) being one of the most important predisposing factors
title: Rhino-Orbital-Cerebral Mucormycosis With Intracranial Extension in a Patient With Diabetic Ketoacidosis.

text: . We report the case of a 44-year-old woman from León, Nicaragua, with poorly controlled type 2 diabetes mellitus who presented with fever, upper respiratory symptoms, palatal ulceration, and progressive orbital involvement. She was admitted in severe DKA and diagnosed with invasive ROCM based on histopathological findings of broad, ribbon-like, aseptate hyphae with right-angle branching
title: Rhino-Orbital-Cerebral Mucormycosis With Intracranial Extension in a Patient With Diabetic Ketoacidosis.

text: . Despite early initiation of amphotericin B and subsequent surgical debridement, the infection proved fatal. This case highlights the need for timely recognition, combined antifungal and surgical management, and optimization of underlying metabolic conditions to improve outcomes in ROCM.
title: Rhino-Orbital-Cerebral Mucormycosis With Intracranial Extension in a Patient With Diabetic Ketoacidosis.

text: Healing or Harming? Navigating Resistance and Rationality in Diabetic Foot Ulcer Antibiotic Therapy: A Retrospective Observational Study.. title: Healing or Harming? Navigating Resistance and Rationality in Diabetic Foot Ulcer Antibiotic Therapy: A Retrospective Observational Study.
journal: Journal of research in pharmacy practice

text: . Our study analyzed the clinical records of 200 patients with DFU selected from a pool of medical records from a tertiary care hospital in India. title: Healing or Harming? Navigating Resistance and Rationality in Diabetic Foot Ulcer Antibiotic Therapy: A Retrospective Observational Study.
journal: Journal of research in pharmacy practice

text: . Antibiotics were the most commonly prescribed drugs (18.5%) with the highest incidence of serious DDIs (28.5%). These results underscore the importance of optimizing antibiotic stewardship and rational prescribing practices to improve clinical outcomes.

text: Glucose excursions throughout the reproductive life stages in women with diabetes.. Women with diabetes experience substantial fluctuations in insulin sensitivity across the reproductive lifespan, yet clinical guidance on managing these glycemic challenges remains limited
title: Glucose excursions throughout the reproductive life stages in women with diabetes.
journal: The Journal of clinical endocrinology and metabolism

text: . This review synthesizes current evidence on the metabolic impact of key hormonal transitions, including puberty, the menstrual cycle, fertility treatment, pregnancy, and menopause, in women with type 1 (T1DM) and type 2 diabetes (T2DM)
title: Glucose excursions throughout the reproductive life stages in women with diabetes.
journal: The Journal of clinical endocrinology and metabolism

text: . Puberty is marked by a physiological decline in insulin sensitivity compounded by behavioral and neurocognitive factors, contributing to dysglycemia and increased cardiometabolic risk. Cyclical variations in estradiol and progesterone influence insulin resistance across the menstrual cycle, but existing data predominantly concern T1DM, leaving major knowledge gaps for T2DM
title: Glucose excursions throughout the reproductive life stages in women with diabetes.
journal: The Journal of clinical endocrinology and metabolism

text: . As fertility treatment becomes more common, understanding the glycemic effects of ovarian stimulation is increasingly important, though current evidence remains sparse
title: Glucose excursions throughout the reproductive life stages in women with diabetes.
journal: The Journal of clinical endocrinology and metabolism

text: . Pregnancy represents a period of pronounced insulin resistance, but advances in diabetes technology, particularly continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) and automated insulin delivery systems, have improved maternal glycemic control and neonatal outcomes and should be integrated into preconception and pregnancy care
title: Glucose excursions throughout the reproductive life stages in women with diabetes.
journal: The Journal of clinical endocrinology and metabolism

text: . In menopause, declining estrogen and relatively preserved androgen levels contribute to increased insulin resistance; menopausal hormone therapy (MHT) may improve glycemia, though evidence in T1DM is limited
title: Glucose excursions throughout the reproductive life stages in women with diabetes.
journal: The Journal of clinical endocrinology and metabolism

text: . Across all life stages, the historical underrepresentation of women in metabolic research has hindered development of evidence-based strategies for managing hormonally driven glucose excursions
title: Glucose excursions throughout the reproductive life stages in women with diabetes.
journal: The Journal of clinical endocrinology and metabolism

text: . Future studies integrating CGM with detailed hormonal profiling, particularly in women with T2DM and those undergoing fertility treatment or MHT, are essential to optimize diabetes care throughout the female lifespan.

text: From Clinical Signs to Functional Recovery: A Practice-Oriented Review of Rotator Cuff Tear Management in Primary Care.. Rotator cuff tear (RCT) is a leading cause of shoulder pain encountered by general practitioners. title: From Clinical Signs to Functional Recovery: A Practice-Oriented Review of Rotator Cuff Tear Management in Primary Care.

text: . This narrative review summarises 105 clinical, imaging, biomechanical and rehabilitation studies published in recent years. The review follows the disorder from early tendinopathy to full-thickness tear and discusses crucial risk factors (age, diabetes, hypercholesterolaemia, overhead work). It aims to guide early primary-care management of RCT
title: From Clinical Signs to Functional Recovery: A Practice-Oriented Review of Rotator Cuff Tear Management in Primary Care.

text: . We examine the diagnostic accuracy of classic bedside tests, including the supraspinatus weakness and external rotation lag cluster. Furthermore, we explain when ultrasound or MRI adds value and what the classic findings are. An informative overview of patient-reported outcome tools (e.g., SPADI, WOSI, Constant-Murley, ASES) could help physicians select one for follow-up
title: From Clinical Signs to Functional Recovery: A Practice-Oriented Review of Rotator Cuff Tear Management in Primary Care.

text: . The article objectively evaluates the evidence for conservative measures-structured exercise protocols, manual therapy, oral analgesics, and corticosteroid or platelet-rich plasma injections. Moreover, we propose an evidence-based postoperative rehabilitation timeline with milestones that incorporate targeted immobilisation and progressive loading
title: From Clinical Signs to Functional Recovery: A Practice-Oriented Review of Rotator Cuff Tear Management in Primary Care.

text: . The article presents selected clinical situations, such as the impact of type 2 diabetes on tendon biology. We explore the viability of experimental adjuncts such as extracorporeal shock-wave therapy, low-intensity pulsed ultrasound and electrical stimulation
title: From Clinical Signs to Functional Recovery: A Practice-Oriented Review of Rotator Cuff Tear Management in Primary Care.

text: . Finally, we compare recommendations from the American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons and the European Society for Surgery of the Shoulder and Elbow. title: From Clinical Signs to Functional Recovery: A Practice-Oriented Review of Rotator Cuff Tear Management in Primary Care.

text: . Our synthesis draws on orthopaedic, radiographic and rehabilitation data to reduce diagnostic delay, optimise non-specialist resource use, and improve pain and functional outcomes for the growing population affected by rotator cuff tears.
title: From Clinical Signs to Functional Recovery: A Practice-Oriented Review of Rotator Cuff Tear Management in Primary Care.

text: From Molecular Mechanisms to Clinical Strategies: A Comprehensive Overview of Metabolic Dysfunction-Associated Steatotic Liver Disease (MASLD).
title: From Molecular Mechanisms to Clinical Strategies: A Comprehensive Overview of Metabolic Dysfunction-Associated Steatotic Liver Disease (MASLD).

text: . Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD), formerly known as non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD), has become one of the most common chronic liver diseases worldwide, representing a major global health challenge closely linked to metabolic syndrome, obesity, and type 2 diabetes mellitus (TD2M)
title: From Molecular Mechanisms to Clinical Strategies: A Comprehensive Overview of Metabolic Dysfunction-Associated Steatotic Liver Disease (MASLD).

text: . The condition is characterized by a multisystem nature driven by complex multifactorial mechanisms, including insulin resistance, lipotoxicity, mitochondrial dysfunction, genetic predispositions, and gut-liver axis alterations. Although liver biopsy remains the gold standard, non-invasive markers and advanced imaging methods are of key importance for early risk stratification
title: From Molecular Mechanisms to Clinical Strategies: A Comprehensive Overview of Metabolic Dysfunction-Associated Steatotic Liver Disease (MASLD).

text: . Furthermore, while liver-related complications such as fibrosis, cirrhosis, and hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) are significant, cardiovascular disease remains the leading cause of mortality in patients with MASLD
title: From Molecular Mechanisms to Clinical Strategies: A Comprehensive Overview of Metabolic Dysfunction-Associated Steatotic Liver Disease (MASLD).

text: . Current management relies primarily on lifestyle modifications, targeted pharmacotherapy (such as pioglitazone, GLP-1 receptor agonists, SGLT-2 inhibitors), and novel experimental therapies. Consequently, MASLD requires a multidisciplinary approach emphasizing early diagnosis, risk stratification, and comprehensive treatment of both hepatic and extrahepatic manifestations.
title: From Molecular Mechanisms to Clinical Strategies: A Comprehensive Overview of Metabolic Dysfunction-Associated Steatotic Liver Disease (MASLD).

text: Patients' Experiences of a Nurse-Guided Physical Activity Program for Type 2 Diabetes and Its Perceived Impact on Health and Quality of Life: A Qualitative Descriptive Study.. title: Patients' Experiences of a Nurse-Guided Physical Activity Program for Type 2 Diabetes and Its Perceived Impact on Health and Quality of Life: A Qualitative Descriptive Study.

title: Patients' Experiences of a Nurse-Guided Physical Activity Program for Type 2 Diabetes and Its Perceived Impact on Health and Quality of Life: A Qualitative Descriptive Study.

text: . To explore the perceived experiences of patients with T2DM participating in a nurse-guided physical activity program and understand its role in improving their health outcomes and quality of life. A qualitative descriptive design was employed
title: Patients' Experiences of a Nurse-Guided Physical Activity Program for Type 2 Diabetes and Its Perceived Impact on Health and Quality of Life: A Qualitative Descriptive Study.

text: . A qualitative descriptive design was employed. Semi-structured interviews were conducted using a 20-item interview guide
title: Patients' Experiences of a Nurse-Guided Physical Activity Program for Type 2 Diabetes and Its Perceived Impact on Health and Quality of Life: A Qualitative Descriptive Study.

text: . Data were analyzed using Braun and Clarke's six-phase reflexive thematic analysis. Trustworthiness was ensured through member checking, peer debriefing, and maintaining an audit trail. The study adhered to the Consolidated Criteria for Reporting Qualitative Research (COREQ) guidelines
title: Patients' Experiences of a Nurse-Guided Physical Activity Program for Type 2 Diabetes and Its Perceived Impact on Health and Quality of Life: A Qualitative Descriptive Study.

text: . Four overarching themes emerged: (1) Transformative Health Journey, encompassing perceived physiological improvements and enhanced energy levels; (2) Psychological Awakening, reflecting improved mood, self-efficacy, and reduced diabetes-related distress; (3) The Pivotal Role of Nursing Support, highlighting the significance of professional guidance, monitoring, and therapeutic relationships; and
title: Patients' Experiences of a Nurse-Guided Physical Activity Program for Type 2 Diabetes and Its Perceived Impact on Health and Quality of Life: A Qualitative Descriptive Study.

text: monitoring, and therapeutic relationships; and (4) Navigating Challenges and Charting Future Directions, addressing barriers, facilitators, and recommendations for program enhancement
title: Patients' Experiences of a Nurse-Guided Physical Activity Program for Type 2 Diabetes and Its Perceived Impact on Health and Quality of Life: A Qualitative Descriptive Study.

text: . Nurse-guided physical activity programs offer multidimensional benefits for patients with T2DM, extending beyond physiological improvements to encompass psychological well-being and lifestyle transformation. Nursing professionals play a critical role in motivating, educating, and supporting patients throughout their health journey
title: Patients' Experiences of a Nurse-Guided Physical Activity Program for Type 2 Diabetes and Its Perceived Impact on Health and Quality of Life: A Qualitative Descriptive Study.

text: . These findings support the integration of nurse-led physical activity interventions into routine diabetes care.
title: Patients' Experiences of a Nurse-Guided Physical Activity Program for Type 2 Diabetes and Its Perceived Impact on Health and Quality of Life: A Qualitative Descriptive Study.

text: Individualized medical nutrition therapy with weekly follow-up improves glycemic control, inflammation, and reduces circulating zonulin in adults with type 2 diabetes mellitus: a randomized controlled trial.
title: Individualized medical nutrition therapy with weekly follow-up improves glycemic control, inflammation, and reduces circulating zonulin in adults with type 2 diabetes mellitus: a randomized controlled trial.

text: Development and Internal Validation of an Explainable Machine Learning Model for Physical Activity Adherence Among Community-Dwelling Patients with Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus.. title: Development and Internal Validation of an Explainable Machine Learning Model for Physical Activity Adherence Among Community-Dwelling Patients with Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus.

text: . This study sought to construct and internally evaluate an interpretable machine learning model for identifying poor physical activity adherence among patients with Type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) in a community-based setting
title: Development and Internal Validation of an Explainable Machine Learning Model for Physical Activity Adherence Among Community-Dwelling Patients with Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus.

text: . Candidate predictors were selected using Elastic Net regularization followed by multivariable logistic regression
title: Development and Internal Validation of an Explainable Machine Learning Model for Physical Activity Adherence Among Community-Dwelling Patients with Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus.

text: . Multiple machine learning algorithms were developed and compared using a randomly allocated training dataset (70%, n = 145) and an internal validation dataset (30%, n = 62). Model discrimination and clinical utility were assessed using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) and decision curve analysis (DCA), respectively
title: Development and Internal Validation of an Explainable Machine Learning Model for Physical Activity Adherence Among Community-Dwelling Patients with Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus.

text: . Shapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) was used to interpret individual predictor contributions to model outputs. Among the 207 participants, 113 (54.6%) demonstrated high physical activity adherence
title: Development and Internal Validation of an Explainable Machine Learning Model for Physical Activity Adherence Among Community-Dwelling Patients with Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus.

text: . The final model incorporated five key predictors: Summary of Diabetes Self-Care Activities (SDSCA) score, estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR_CKD-EPI_2009), family history of diabetes, International Physical Activity Questionnaire (IPAQ) score, and albumin (ALB)
title: Development and Internal Validation of an Explainable Machine Learning Model for Physical Activity Adherence Among Community-Dwelling Patients with Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus.

text: . The SVM model achieved the highest discrimination ability among the tested algorithms and was subsequently selected as the final model (AUC = 0.787, 95% CI: 0.671-0.903). SHAP analysis provided transparent visualization of the relative contribution of each predictor to model outputs
title: Development and Internal Validation of an Explainable Machine Learning Model for Physical Activity Adherence Among Community-Dwelling Patients with Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus.

text: . This study provides an explainable machine learning approach for identifying key variables associated with physical activity adherence among individuals with T2DM in community diabetes management. Further validation in independent populations is needed before the model can be considered for risk assessment and personalized behavioral intervention planning in community diabetes care.
title: Development and Internal Validation of an Explainable Machine Learning Model for Physical Activity Adherence Among Community-Dwelling Patients with Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus.

text: Effects of Renin-Angiotensin Inhibitors, Sodium-Glucose Cotransporter 2 Inhibitors, Mineralocorticoid Receptor Antagonists and Glucagon-Like Peptide 1 Receptor Agonists on Kidney Outcomes in Patients With Type 1 Diabetes: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
title: Effects of Renin-Angiotensin Inhibitors, Sodium-Glucose Cotransporter 2 Inhibitors, Mineralocorticoid Receptor Antagonists and Glucagon-Like Peptide 1 Receptor Agonists on Kidney Outcomes in Patients With Type 1 Diabetes: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.

text: . While the new kidney protective therapies have transformed chronic kidney disease (CKD) management in patients with Type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM), treatment options for CKD in Type 1 diabetes mellitus (T1DM) have remained unchanged for 30 years, limited to renin-angiotensin system inhibitors (RASis)
title: Effects of Renin-Angiotensin Inhibitors, Sodium-Glucose Cotransporter 2 Inhibitors, Mineralocorticoid Receptor Antagonists and Glucagon-Like Peptide 1 Receptor Agonists on Kidney Outcomes in Patients With Type 1 Diabetes: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.

text: . Given similarities in pathophysiology between CKD in T1DM and T2DM, we conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis evaluating sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitors (SGLT-2is), mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists (MRAs) and glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RAs) on kidney function, albuminuria and safety outcomes
title: Effects of Renin-Angiotensin Inhibitors, Sodium-Glucose Cotransporter 2 Inhibitors, Mineralocorticoid Receptor Antagonists and Glucagon-Like Peptide 1 Receptor Agonists on Kidney Outcomes in Patients With Type 1 Diabetes: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.

text: . We searched Medline, EMBASE, Cochrane CENTRAL, CINAHL, Global Health, LILACS and Scopus from inception until 11 April 2025, for randomised controlled trials (RCTs) evaluating RASi, MRAs, GLP-1RAs and SGLT-2is on change in urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio (UACR) and estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) in adults (age ≥ 18) with T1DM
title: Effects of Renin-Angiotensin Inhibitors, Sodium-Glucose Cotransporter 2 Inhibitors, Mineralocorticoid Receptor Antagonists and Glucagon-Like Peptide 1 Receptor Agonists on Kidney Outcomes in Patients With Type 1 Diabetes: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.

text: . A total of 7151 unique records were identified and 41 RCTs were included in the meta-analysis. No RCTs evaluating nsMRAs or MRAs met our inclusion criteria. Treatment with SGLT-2i or RASi was associated with a 45% reduction in UACR versus placebo (GMR = 0.55; 95% CI: 0.32-0.94)
title: Effects of Renin-Angiotensin Inhibitors, Sodium-Glucose Cotransporter 2 Inhibitors, Mineralocorticoid Receptor Antagonists and Glucagon-Like Peptide 1 Receptor Agonists on Kidney Outcomes in Patients With Type 1 Diabetes: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.

text: . No difference in the annual rate of eGFR change was observed across drug classes compared to placebo (mean difference 1.16 mL/min/1.73 m In patients with T1DM, the pooled analysis showed a reduction in UACR overall, but that this appeared to be driven predominantly by the SGLT-2i studies, with limited and non-significant evidence in the RAS inhibitor subgroup

text: Effects of a Nurse-Led Diabetes Perception Intervention Delivered via a Mobile Messaging Platform (LINE) on Glycemic Control and Patient Outcomes Among Adults with Diabetes and Poorly Controlled Glucose: A Randomized Controlled Trial.. title: Effects of a Nurse-Led Diabetes Perception Intervention Delivered via a Mobile Messaging Platform (LINE) on Glycemic Control and Patient Outcomes Among Adults with Diabetes and Poorly Controlled Glucose: A Randomized Controlled Trial.

text: . Illness perceptions may influence diabetes self-management behaviors and glycemic control. title: Effects of a Nurse-Led Diabetes Perception Intervention Delivered via a Mobile Messaging Platform (LINE) on Glycemic Control and Patient Outcomes Among Adults with Diabetes and Poorly Controlled Glucose: A Randomized Controlled Trial.

text: . HbA1c, FPG, and patient satisfaction were assessed at baseline and week 13, and illness perceptions at baseline, week 6, and week 13. Data were analyzed using analysis of covariance and repeated-measures analysis of variance. Baseline characteristics were comparable between groups

text: Recognizing Euglycemic Diabetic Ketoacidosis in the Era of SGLT2 Inhibitors: A Case Report.. Euglycemic diabetic ketoacidosis (euDKA) is an increasingly recognized complication associated with SGLT2 inhibitors. Because serum glucose levels may remain normal or only mildly elevated, diagnosis can be delayed, potentially increasing morbidity
title: Recognizing Euglycemic Diabetic Ketoacidosis in the Era of SGLT2 Inhibitors: A Case Report.

text: . We present the case of a 51-year-old male with long-standing poorly controlled type 2 diabetes mellitus who developed euDKA shortly after initiation of empagliflozin/metformin therapy. title: Recognizing Euglycemic Diabetic Ketoacidosis in the Era of SGLT2 Inhibitors: A Case Report.

text: . Initial laboratory evaluation revealed high anion gap metabolic acidosis with positive urinary ketones and a glucose level of 160 mg/dL. Infectious workup was negative. title: Recognizing Euglycemic Diabetic Ketoacidosis in the Era of SGLT2 Inhibitors: A Case Report.

text: . This case adds to the growing body of literature describing euDKA in patients receiving SGLT2 inhibitor therapy in the setting of reduced oral intake and poorly controlled diabetes mellitus.
title: Recognizing Euglycemic Diabetic Ketoacidosis in the Era of SGLT2 Inhibitors: A Case Report.

text: A Simple Scoring Model for Mid-term Remission of Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus After Sleeve Gastrectomy in Chinese Patients.. Metabolic bariatric surgery is the most effective treatment for obesity and related type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM), but T2DM remission post-surgery is heterogeneous
title: A Simple Scoring Model for Mid-term Remission of Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus After Sleeve Gastrectomy in Chinese Patients.

text: . title: A Simple Scoring Model for Mid-term Remission of Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus After Sleeve Gastrectomy in Chinese Patients.

text: . We performed a retrospective cohort study of Chinese patients with obesity and T2DM who underwent primary LSG between 2017 and 2023. title: A Simple Scoring Model for Mid-term Remission of Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus After Sleeve Gastrectomy in Chinese Patients.

text: . The final model was simplified into a scoring system. The final model retained three predictors: number of hypoglycemic agents, insulin use, and 2-hour plasma C-peptide, and showed strong discrimination (AUC 0.876)
title: A Simple Scoring Model for Mid-term Remission of Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus After Sleeve Gastrectomy in Chinese Patients.

text: . Bootstrap validation confirmed robust performance (mean AUC 0.878, 95% CI 0.809-0.935). The simplified score (2-hour plasma C-peptide-5 × number of hypoglycemic agents - insulin use score [11/0]) showed the same AUC, and higher scores indicated greater remission probability
title: A Simple Scoring Model for Mid-term Remission of Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus After Sleeve Gastrectomy in Chinese Patients.

text: . We developed and internally validated a preoperative model for predicting mid-term T2DM remission after LSG in Chinese patients with obesity and T2DM. The model was translated into a simple scoring system that may support individualized management and decision-making.
