text: Development of autoencoder-guided attention-LSTM models for predicting nocturnal hypoglycemia risk in Type 1 Diabetes.. Nocturnal hypoglycemia (NH) is a major, often undetected risk for individuals with Type 1 Diabetes (T1DM). Current prediction models lack sufficient lead time for proactive, pre-sleep interventions
title: Development of autoencoder-guided attention-LSTM models for predicting nocturnal hypoglycemia risk in Type 1 Diabetes.

text: . This study develops a novel, interpretable deep learning approach for predicting NH events up to 12 hours in advance. We propose a hybrid model that infuses physiological knowledge (simulated glucose absorption, insulin kinetics, and subcellular insulin signaling) into an attention-based Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) network
title: Development of autoencoder-guided attention-LSTM models for predicting nocturnal hypoglycemia risk in Type 1 Diabetes.

text: . An Autoencoder-based Attention Weight Mapping (A2WM) framework is introduced to trace model attention back to the original 24-hour inputs (CGM, meals, insulin) for interpretability. The model was developed using the OhioT1DM dataset (open-loop pump users) and externally validated on the SMARTDIAB dataset (open-loop pump users)
title: Development of autoencoder-guided attention-LSTM models for predicting nocturnal hypoglycemia risk in Type 1 Diabetes.

text: . On the OhioT1DM test set, the model achieved an AUC of 0.9387, recall of 0.9333, and specificity of 0.8548. On the external SMARTDIAB cohort, it demonstrated robust generalizability, achieving an AUC of 0.8684, recall of 0.6316, and specificity of 0.9615. Decision Curve Analysis confirmed a high net clinical benefit, and the A2WM interpretations identified clinically relevant temporal features
title: Development of autoencoder-guided attention-LSTM models for predicting nocturnal hypoglycemia risk in Type 1 Diabetes.

text: . The proposed physiologically-informed, attention based LSTM model can accurately and interpretably predict 12 hour NH risk from historical data and scheduled basal insulin
title: Development of autoencoder-guided attention-LSTM models for predicting nocturnal hypoglycemia risk in Type 1 Diabetes.

text: . This work provides a clinically valuable tool for proactive NH management, offering an extended lead time that empowers T1DM patients to implement preventive strategies (e.g., pre-sleep meal or insulin adjustments) well before hypoglycemia occurs.
title: Development of autoencoder-guided attention-LSTM models for predicting nocturnal hypoglycemia risk in Type 1 Diabetes.

text: Five-year outcomes of single-anastomosis duodeno-ileal bypass with sleeve gastrectomy (SADI-S) in adults with type 1 diabetes mellitus.. Managing obesity in adults with type 1 diabetes mellitus (T1DM) is challenging because insulin dependence often coexists with significant insulin resistance. While metabolic surgery is well established in type 2 diabetes, long-term data in T1DM remain limited
title: Five-year outcomes of single-anastomosis duodeno-ileal bypass with sleeve gastrectomy (SADI-S) in adults with type 1 diabetes mellitus.

text: . This study evaluates five-year outcomes of single-anastomosis duodeno-ileal bypass with sleeve gastrectomy (SADI-S) in adults with T1DM. Adults with T1DM and obesity who underwent primary SADI-S at a single center were followed for up to five years
title: Five-year outcomes of single-anastomosis duodeno-ileal bypass with sleeve gastrectomy (SADI-S) in adults with type 1 diabetes mellitus.

text: . Outcomes included weight, BMI, HbA1c, total daily insulin requirements, continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) metrics, nutritional status, peri-operative safety, and patient-reported quality-of-life measures. CGM data were analyzed for time in range, glycemic variability, time above range, and time below range
title: Five-year outcomes of single-anastomosis duodeno-ileal bypass with sleeve gastrectomy (SADI-S) in adults with type 1 diabetes mellitus.

text: . Patient-reported outcomes included the SF-12, Diabetes Treatment Satisfaction Questionnaire, and BAROS. Eight patients contributed five-year outcome data. Mean BMI decreased from 38.6 kg/m² to 26.4 kg/m². HbA1c improved from 8.4% to 7.1%, and total daily insulin requirements decreased by approximately 45%
title: Five-year outcomes of single-anastomosis duodeno-ileal bypass with sleeve gastrectomy (SADI-S) in adults with type 1 diabetes mellitus.

text: . CGM data demonstrated increased time in range, reduced glycemic variability, and stable rates of hypoglycemia. Quality-of-life scores improved across all validated domains. Two cases of early postoperative euglycemic diabetic ketoacidosis occurred before implementation of extended inpatient monitoring; none occurred thereafter
title: Five-year outcomes of single-anastomosis duodeno-ileal bypass with sleeve gastrectomy (SADI-S) in adults with type 1 diabetes mellitus.

text: . No patient developed protein-calorie malnutrition or severe micronutrient deficiency. SADI-S produced sustained weight loss, improved glycemic stability, reduced insulin requirements, and acceptable nutritional outcomes over five years in adults with T1DM. These findings support SADI-S as a physiologically favorable metabolic procedure in carefully selected insulin-treated individuals.
title: Five-year outcomes of single-anastomosis duodeno-ileal bypass with sleeve gastrectomy (SADI-S) in adults with type 1 diabetes mellitus.

text: Prevalence and determinants of inpatient hypoglycemia among hospitalized adults with diabetes: a cohort study.. Inpatient hypoglycemia is a serious yet often under-recognized threat to the safety and well-being of hospitalized people with diabetes. Evidence on its prevalence and predictors in non-critical care settings remains limited
title: Prevalence and determinants of inpatient hypoglycemia among hospitalized adults with diabetes: a cohort study.

text: . This study aimed to determine the prevalence and predictors of inpatient hypoglycemia among hospitalized adults with diabetes. This is a two-center, retrospective cohort study involving 1,945 adult inpatients with diabetes admitted to non-critical wards in two tertiary hospitals in 2024
title: Prevalence and determinants of inpatient hypoglycemia among hospitalized adults with diabetes: a cohort study.

text: . Participants were retrospectively followed from admission till discharge, while exposure to independent variables and hypoglycemia events were recorded. Multivariable logistic regression was employed to identify independent risk factors for hypoglycemia. The prevalence of inpatient hypoglycemia was 19.7% and was associated with a significantly prolonged hospital stay (median 8 vs
title: Prevalence and determinants of inpatient hypoglycemia among hospitalized adults with diabetes: a cohort study.

text: . 6 days;  Inpatient hypoglycemia remains a clinically significant complication associated with prolonged hospitalization. Key risk factors, interactions, and protective factors were identified. These provide critical data to guide risk-stratified care and enhance patient safety.
title: Prevalence and determinants of inpatient hypoglycemia among hospitalized adults with diabetes: a cohort study.

text: Use of Automated Insulin Delivery Systems in the Immediate Postpartum Period.. Automated insulin delivery (AID) systems are increasingly used in pregnant people with type 1 diabetes, yet the necessary guidance for use during the immediate postpartum period is not well established
title: Use of Automated Insulin Delivery Systems in the Immediate Postpartum Period.

text: . A 30-year-old-nulliparous woman with type 1 diabetes presented at 36 weeks gestation with spontaneous rupture of membranes. She used Omnipod® 5 system in automated mode with a glucose target of 110 mg/dL (6.6 mmol/L) due to her high glucose variability, history of hypoglycemia, and personal preference
title: Use of Automated Insulin Delivery Systems in the Immediate Postpartum Period.

text: . She underwent caesarian section with glycemia managed by continuous intravenous insulin but resumed AID immediately postpartum. Prior to delivery, she required approximately 37 units of basal insulin daily but experienced multiple hypoglycemic episodes and frequent suspension of basal insulin after giving birth, with 8.9 units of basal insulin delivered on postpartum day one
title: Use of Automated Insulin Delivery Systems in the Immediate Postpartum Period.

text: . It can take 2 weeks for the Omnipod® 5 algorithm to acknowledge reduced insulin needs. Despite proactive adjustments, she experienced intermittent hypoglycemia until her carbohydrate ratio was decreased, and target glucose was increased to 140 mg/dL (7.8 mmol/L) on postpartum day four
title: Use of Automated Insulin Delivery Systems in the Immediate Postpartum Period.

text: . Although not extensively studied, potential strategies to mitigate hypoglycemia in people using AID in the postpartum period include resetting the device, using the activity feature, increasing target glucose and adjusting sensitivity and carbohydrate ratio, or switching from automated to manual mode
title: Use of Automated Insulin Delivery Systems in the Immediate Postpartum Period.

text: . This case highlights the need for further investigation regarding optimal procedures to safely manage people with type 1 diabetes using AID in the postpartum period.
title: Use of Automated Insulin Delivery Systems in the Immediate Postpartum Period.

text: Interdisciplinary Management of Concussion in an Adolescent With Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus: Diagnostic Challenges Related to Hypoglycemia and Cognitive Impairment.. Type 1 diabetes mellitus (T1DM) can complicate recovery after mild traumatic brain injury (mTBI) by mimicking post-concussive symptoms
title: Interdisciplinary Management of Concussion in an Adolescent With Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus: Diagnostic Challenges Related to Hypoglycemia and Cognitive Impairment.

text: . This case details the recovery of a 17-year-old female with T1DM who sustained an mTBI and lumbar spine fractures following a motor vehicle collision. Post-traumatic amnesia, short-term memory deficits, and impaired glucose regulation complicated her recovery
title: Interdisciplinary Management of Concussion in an Adolescent With Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus: Diagnostic Challenges Related to Hypoglycemia and Cognitive Impairment.

text: . Cognitive symptoms of mTBI, such as working memory and attention deficits, can be worsened by nocturnal hypoglycemia, increasing the risk of poor glycemic control due to challenges with dietary and insulin management. Additionally, mTBI symptoms, such as headache and irritability, can overlap with hypoglycemia
title: Interdisciplinary Management of Concussion in an Adolescent With Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus: Diagnostic Challenges Related to Hypoglycemia and Cognitive Impairment.

text: . At her one-week Physical Medicine and Rehabilitation (PM&R) follow-up, she reported persistent daily headaches, fatigue, neck pain, and nightly glucose readings in the 40s. In addition to standard concussion follow-up, the primary team coordinated a same-day evaluation by pediatric endocrinology, allowing real-time insulin adjustment in the clinic
title: Interdisciplinary Management of Concussion in an Adolescent With Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus: Diagnostic Challenges Related to Hypoglycemia and Cognitive Impairment.

text: . With interdisciplinary management, the patient returned to her pre-injury cognitive baseline, her headaches improved, and her glucose levels stabilized. Misattributing symptoms to either mTBI or hypoglycemia can delay targeted treatment for both conditions, leading to worse functional outcomes and a prolonged rehabilitation course
title: Interdisciplinary Management of Concussion in an Adolescent With Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus: Diagnostic Challenges Related to Hypoglycemia and Cognitive Impairment.

text: . This case highlights the importance of glycemic monitoring and team-based management in adolescents with T1DM recovering from concussion. It also illustrates the absence of standardized management strategies for adolescents with concurrent mTBI and T1DM.
title: Interdisciplinary Management of Concussion in an Adolescent With Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus: Diagnostic Challenges Related to Hypoglycemia and Cognitive Impairment.

text: Driving-Related Glucose Monitoring Practices Among Insulin-Treated Adults With Type 2 Diabetes.. Driving requires complex cognitive, motor, and sensory coordination, all of which may be adversely affected by diabetes. For individuals treated with insulin, hypoglycemia represents the principal safety concern
title: Driving-Related Glucose Monitoring Practices Among Insulin-Treated Adults With Type 2 Diabetes.
journal: Journal of diabetes science and technology

text: . Although many jurisdictions provide guidance for insulin-treated drivers, adherence to these recommendations remains unclear. An online survey was conducted among 500 licensed drivers with insulin-requiring type 2 diabetes (T2D) from the United States and the United Kingdom, not using continuous glucose monitoring (CGM)
title: Driving-Related Glucose Monitoring Practices Among Insulin-Treated Adults With Type 2 Diabetes.
journal: Journal of diabetes science and technology

text: . The survey included discrete and open-ended questions relating to diabetes management and driving behaviors. Descriptive and inferential statistical analyses were performed. Participants were predominantly male (59%, n = 293) with a mean T2D duration of eight years
title: Driving-Related Glucose Monitoring Practices Among Insulin-Treated Adults With Type 2 Diabetes.
journal: Journal of diabetes science and technology

text: . Insulin regimens included basal-only therapy (54%, n = 257), multiple daily injections (39%, n = 197), and continuous subcutaneous insulin infusion (9%, n = 46). Severe hypoglycemic event(s) in the preceding 12 months were reported by 34%, and 54% had evidence of impaired awareness of hypoglycemia (Clarke score >4)
title: Driving-Related Glucose Monitoring Practices Among Insulin-Treated Adults With Type 2 Diabetes.
journal: Journal of diabetes science and technology

text: . Furthermore, 37% (n = 185) limited their driving due to insulin-related concerns, and 72% (n = 359) worried particularly about hypoglycemia. Only 34% (n = 168) reported checking glucose levels before driving >75% of the time. If feeling hypo before driving, 59% (n = 295) would take a snack but drive immediately
title: Driving-Related Glucose Monitoring Practices Among Insulin-Treated Adults With Type 2 Diabetes.
journal: Journal of diabetes science and technology

text: . If feeling hypoglycemic while driving, 10% (n = 48) would attempt to 'get to their destination fast'. Only 27% (n = 138) carried fast-acting carbohydrates, and 42% (n = 210) felt safe to drive 'as soon as I feel better' while 32% (n = 163) would 'wait 45 minutes and recheck their glucose levels'. Potentially unsafe driving behaviors are common among adults with insulin-treated T2D
title: Driving-Related Glucose Monitoring Practices Among Insulin-Treated Adults With Type 2 Diabetes.
journal: Journal of diabetes science and technology

text: . There appears to be a need to improve the understanding of safe driving guidance.
title: Driving-Related Glucose Monitoring Practices Among Insulin-Treated Adults With Type 2 Diabetes.
journal: Journal of diabetes science and technology

text: Electronic health record-derived machine learning model for hypoglycemia risk prediction in type 2 diabetes mellitus patients: development and validation.. Hypoglycemia is a serious complication of diabetes. Early recognition of hypoglycemia can improve clinical prognosis, however, traditional diagnostic tools are often limited
title: Electronic health record-derived machine learning model for hypoglycemia risk prediction in type 2 diabetes mellitus patients: development and validation.

text: . Machine learning offers a promising approach for predicting adverse outcomes in diabetic patients. This study aims to develop and validate machine learning-based models to predict the risk of hypoglycemia in type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) patients. A cohort study design was employed. Clinical data were collected from the electronic health record system
title: Electronic health record-derived machine learning model for hypoglycemia risk prediction in type 2 diabetes mellitus patients: development and validation.

text: . The dataset was randomly partitioned into training and validation subsets using a 7:3 ratio. Four machine learning algorithms, logistic regression (LR), Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost), random forest (RF), and support vector machine (SVM) were implemented to develop hypoglycemia risk prediction models
title: Electronic health record-derived machine learning model for hypoglycemia risk prediction in type 2 diabetes mellitus patients: development and validation.

text: . Predictive performance was assessed using sensitivity, specificity, accuracy, precision, F1 score, and the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC). 831 T2DM patients were included, the hypoglycemia incidence was 22.0%
title: Electronic health record-derived machine learning model for hypoglycemia risk prediction in type 2 diabetes mellitus patients: development and validation.

text: . In the training cohort, the AUC for the LR, XGBoost, SVM, and RF models were 0.82, 0.86, 0.84, and 0.80, and corresponding AUCs were 0.76, 0.78, 0.72, and 0.75 in the validation cohort. The XGBoost demonstrated the highest overall predictive performance
title: Electronic health record-derived machine learning model for hypoglycemia risk prediction in type 2 diabetes mellitus patients: development and validation.

text: . Feature importance analysis based on the XGBoost model identified creatinine, triglycerides, albumin, HbA1c, C-peptide, aspartate aminotransferase, hemoglobin, and sulfonylurea use as the most influential predictors of hypoglycemia risk. The XGBoost model exhibited superior predictive performance for achieving the higher AUC, F1 score, greater accuracy, sensitivity and specificity
title: Electronic health record-derived machine learning model for hypoglycemia risk prediction in type 2 diabetes mellitus patients: development and validation.

text: . This model enables effective identification of T2DM patients who may require intensified monitoring or targeted interventions to prevent hypoglycemic events. Not applicable.
title: Electronic health record-derived machine learning model for hypoglycemia risk prediction in type 2 diabetes mellitus patients: development and validation.

text: Continuous glucose monitoring reveals improved hyperglycemia and altered hypoglycemia target attainment after gastrectomy in patients with type 2 diabetes.
title: Continuous glucose monitoring reveals improved hyperglycemia and altered hypoglycemia target attainment after gastrectomy in patients with type 2 diabetes.

text: . This study aimed to investigate glycemic variability and biochemical profiles before and after gastrectomy using continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) and to evaluate whether postoperative improvements occur in blood glucose levels and biochemical parameters. We analyzed data from patients who underwent surgery for gastric cancer
title: Continuous glucose monitoring reveals improved hyperglycemia and altered hypoglycemia target attainment after gastrectomy in patients with type 2 diabetes.

text: . Glucose profiles were assessed using a CGM device before gastrectomy and after discharge. All patients discontinued antidiabetic medications one day before surgery and resumed them only after reassessment at outpatient follow-up
title: Continuous glucose monitoring reveals improved hyperglycemia and altered hypoglycemia target attainment after gastrectomy in patients with type 2 diabetes.

text: . CGM-derived metrics were evaluated according to international consensus recommendations, including time above range (TAR), time below range (TBR), time in range (TIR), CV (coefficient of variation), and MAGE (mean amplitude of glycemic excursions). A total of 33 patients were included. The mean duration of diabetes was 16.9 ± 10.4 years, and 12.1% were receiving insulin therapy
title: Continuous glucose monitoring reveals improved hyperglycemia and altered hypoglycemia target attainment after gastrectomy in patients with type 2 diabetes.

text: . Mean glucose levels and TAR significantly decreased after gastrectomy while TIR significantly increased. Although TBR did not increase significantly, adherence to hypoglycemia targets worsened postoperatively. Glucose variability, assessed by CV, remained stable. Also, most patients maintained CV values below the threshold for glycemic instability
title: Continuous glucose monitoring reveals improved hyperglycemia and altered hypoglycemia target attainment after gastrectomy in patients with type 2 diabetes.

text: . MAGE significantly decreased after surgery, indicating a reduction in large-amplitude glucose excursions. Among 16 patients whose postoperative medication changes were evaluated, seven (43.8%) reduced their antidiabetic medication after gastrectomy
title: Continuous glucose monitoring reveals improved hyperglycemia and altered hypoglycemia target attainment after gastrectomy in patients with type 2 diabetes.

text: . In conclusion, despite the temporary discontinuation of antidiabetic medications, hyperglycemia improved without aggravation of glycemic variability, as reflected by increased TIR, stable CV and reduced MAGE. However, the achievement of hypoglycemia targets was reduced
title: Continuous glucose monitoring reveals improved hyperglycemia and altered hypoglycemia target attainment after gastrectomy in patients with type 2 diabetes.

text: . Therefore, instead of routinely resuming preoperative antidiabetic regimens, postoperative glucose management should be individualized based on CGM-derived glycemic profiles.
title: Continuous glucose monitoring reveals improved hyperglycemia and altered hypoglycemia target attainment after gastrectomy in patients with type 2 diabetes.

text: Diabetes distress: What a clinician needs to know - A South Asian perspective.. Diabetes distress (DD) is a phenomenon that highlights the emotional strain of having diabetes and the unrelenting demands of this illness; DD is very high and known in a poorly studied area of South Asia
title: Diabetes distress: What a clinician needs to know - A South Asian perspective.
journal: Best practice & research. Clinical endocrinology & metabolism

text: . This review is based on evidence published since 2023 and provides an enhancement of the 2023 South Asian Federation of Endocrine Societies (SAFES) recommendations. A 2025 systematic review and meta-analysis found pooled prevalence of type 2 diabetes distress of 85% in Pakistan, 42% in India and Bangladesh and 25% in Sri Lanka with emotional burden turning out to be the prevailing domain
title: Diabetes distress: What a clinician needs to know - A South Asian perspective.
journal: Best practice & research. Clinical endocrinology & metabolism

text: . The predictors of increased distress are always female gender, low socioeconomic status, prolonged period of the disease, comorbidities and poor glycemic control
title: Diabetes distress: What a clinician needs to know - A South Asian perspective.
journal: Best practice & research. Clinical endocrinology & metabolism

text: . Qualitative research indicates that South Asian patients are distressed due to family strain, out-of-pocket expenditure compelling them to decide whether to purchase the drug or not and fragmented health systems that isolate mental and physical health care
title: Diabetes distress: What a clinician needs to know - A South Asian perspective.
journal: Best practice & research. Clinical endocrinology & metabolism

text: . Cultural factors such as gendered roles in care giving, limited resources in the household budget and lack of social support increase emotional load and limit self-management
title: Diabetes distress: What a clinician needs to know - A South Asian perspective.
journal: Best practice & research. Clinical endocrinology & metabolism

text: . Clinicians can deal with diabetes distress by screening with validated measures and including short-term psychosocial counseling with diabetes visits, simplifying regimens to minimize hypoglycemia, addressing social support shortfalls and promoting care that is gender-sensitive and affordable
title: Diabetes distress: What a clinician needs to know - A South Asian perspective.
journal: Best practice & research. Clinical endocrinology & metabolism

text: . The review can guide South Asian clinicians to identify, evaluate and act on diabetes distress in resource limited, culturally diverse environments which will in turn enhance the glycemic and quality of life outcomes.
title: Diabetes distress: What a clinician needs to know - A South Asian perspective.
journal: Best practice & research. Clinical endocrinology & metabolism

text: Cardiovascular Risk Reduction With Tirzepatide, a Dual GIP/GLP-1 Agonist, in Patients With Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus.. Tirzepatide is the first dual glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide/glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptor agonist to be approved for the treatment of diabetes mellitus
title: Cardiovascular Risk Reduction With Tirzepatide, a Dual GIP/GLP-1 Agonist, in Patients With Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus.

text: . The SURPASS trials investigated the efficacy and safety of tirzepatide, both as monotherapy and as add-on therapy, in comparison with placebo, basal insulin, semaglutide, or dulaglutide in patients with type 2 diabetes
title: Cardiovascular Risk Reduction With Tirzepatide, a Dual GIP/GLP-1 Agonist, in Patients With Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus.

text: . Tirzepatide at doses of 5 mg, 10 mg, or 15 mg produced significant reductions in hemoglobin A1c levels (-1.87% to -2.58%) and body weight (-6.2 to -12.9 kg) in patients with type 2 diabetes, without increasing the risk of serious hypoglycemia. Tirzepatide also improved lipid parameters and lowered blood pressure
title: Cardiovascular Risk Reduction With Tirzepatide, a Dual GIP/GLP-1 Agonist, in Patients With Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus.

text: . Most of the observed adverse events were mild gastrointestinal symptoms, and the occurrence rate of these events was comparable to that associated with GLP-1 receptor agonists such as semaglutide (1 mg) or dulaglutide (0.75 mg)
title: Cardiovascular Risk Reduction With Tirzepatide, a Dual GIP/GLP-1 Agonist, in Patients With Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus.

text: . In this review, we summarize the pharmacodynamics and pharmacokinetics of tirzepatide, review the findings from the phase III SURPASS clinical trials, and discuss the anticipated beneficial effects of tirzepatide on the prevention and management of atherosclerosis and dyslipidemia in patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus.
title: Cardiovascular Risk Reduction With Tirzepatide, a Dual GIP/GLP-1 Agonist, in Patients With Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus.

text: Effectiveness and Safety of Semaglutide in Type 1 Diabetes: A Danish Nationwide Cohort Study (2018-2024).. Semaglutide is not approved for glycemic management in type 1 diabetes (T1D) due to limited evidence and safety concerns. Nevertheless, its use is increasing. We investigated glycemic and safety outcomes of semaglutide in a nationwide cohort of individuals with T1D
title: Effectiveness and Safety of Semaglutide in Type 1 Diabetes: A Danish Nationwide Cohort Study (2018-2024).

text: . Using Danish registries (2018-2024), we identified individuals with T1D initiating semaglutide and matched them 1:4 using exposure density matching to unexposed control persons with T1D following them for up to two years. Glycemic trajectories were modeled using a piecewise mixed model
title: Effectiveness and Safety of Semaglutide in Type 1 Diabetes: A Danish Nationwide Cohort Study (2018-2024).

text: . Cause-specific Cox models were used to estimate hospitalization rates for hypoglycemia and diabetic ketoacidosis compared with matched controls. Aalen-Johansen estimator was used to estimate adherence while accounting for death as a competing risk. We identified 879 individuals with T1D initiating semaglutide (multiple daily injections (MDI): n = 622; insulin pump: n = 257)
title: Effectiveness and Safety of Semaglutide in Type 1 Diabetes: A Danish Nationwide Cohort Study (2018-2024).

text: . HbA1c decreased by 5.7 mmol/mol (0.52%) (95% CI: 5.0-6.3) during the first six months and remained stable thereafter in semaglutide users while remaining unchanged in the control group. Compared with matched controls semaglutide use was not associated with an increased rate of hospitalization for hypoglycemia (HR 0.64; 95%CI: 0.35; 1.19) or diabetic ketoacidosis (HR 0.73; 95%CI; 0.34; 1.57)
title: Effectiveness and Safety of Semaglutide in Type 1 Diabetes: A Danish Nationwide Cohort Study (2018-2024).

text: . The cumulative probability of adherence to semaglutide at one year was 50% (95% CI: 47-54). No difference in HbA1c reduction from 0 to 6 months was observed between MDI compared to insulin pump users (P = 0.42). The median semaglutide dose redeemed during follow-up was 1.0 mg
title: Effectiveness and Safety of Semaglutide in Type 1 Diabetes: A Danish Nationwide Cohort Study (2018-2024).

text: . In this nationwide cohort of individuals with T1D, semaglutide use was associated with no increased rate of hospitalization for hypoglycemia and no increased diabetic ketoacidosis rate, and a clinically meaningful reduction of HbA1c. This study received no funding.
title: Effectiveness and Safety of Semaglutide in Type 1 Diabetes: A Danish Nationwide Cohort Study (2018-2024).

text: Intrapartum and Early Postpartum Use of Automated Insulin Delivery in Type 1 Diabetes: A Prespecified Analysis of the CIRCUIT Randomized Controlled Trial.
title: Intrapartum and Early Postpartum Use of Automated Insulin Delivery in Type 1 Diabetes: A Prespecified Analysis of the CIRCUIT Randomized Controlled Trial.

text: . Following the demonstrated improvement in pregnancy glycemia with Control-IQ closed loop in the Closed-Loop Insulin Delivery by Glucose Responsive Computer Algorithms in Type 1 Diabetes Pregnancies (CIRCUIT) trial, we compared intrapartum and early postpartum glycemic effectiveness and safety with standard care in type 1 diabetes
title: Intrapartum and Early Postpartum Use of Automated Insulin Delivery in Type 1 Diabetes: A Prespecified Analysis of the CIRCUIT Randomized Controlled Trial.

text: . The primary outcome of this prespecified analysis was percentage of time in pregnancy-specific glucose range (63-140 mg/dL) during the 24 h prior to childbirth, measured by continuous glucose monitoring
title: Intrapartum and Early Postpartum Use of Automated Insulin Delivery in Type 1 Diabetes: A Prespecified Analysis of the CIRCUIT Randomized Controlled Trial.

text: . A key secondary outcome was percentage of time at <70 mg/dL in the first postpartum week, with additional secondary outcomes including continuous glucose monitoring metrics through 6 weeks postpartum. Analyses were adjusted for baseline measure, insulin delivery mode, and site. In the intrapartum period (24 h before delivery), 39 of 44 (89%) participants continued closed loop
title: Intrapartum and Early Postpartum Use of Automated Insulin Delivery in Type 1 Diabetes: A Prespecified Analysis of the CIRCUIT Randomized Controlled Trial.

text: . Intravenous insulin was used intrapartum by one (2%) closed-loop participant and 20 (45%) standard-care participants (P < 0.001). Intrapartum closed-loop users spent more time in pregnancy-specific glucose range (79.6% vs. 64.8%) than the standard-care group (mean adjusted difference 13.2 percentage points; 95% CI 5.2, 21.2)
title: Intrapartum and Early Postpartum Use of Automated Insulin Delivery in Type 1 Diabetes: A Prespecified Analysis of the CIRCUIT Randomized Controlled Trial.

text: . In the first postpartum week, the closed-loop group spent less time <70 mg/dL (1.7% vs. 3.2%; mean adjusted difference -1.8 percentage points; 95% CI -0.9 to -2.7) compared with the standard-care group. No maternal severe hypoglycemia occurred in the closed-loop group, while one episode occurred in the standard-care group postpartum. No diabetic ketoacidosis occurred in either group
title: Intrapartum and Early Postpartum Use of Automated Insulin Delivery in Type 1 Diabetes: A Prespecified Analysis of the CIRCUIT Randomized Controlled Trial.

text: . Use of this closed-loop system resulted in superior intrapartum and early postpartum glycemia compared with standard care without safety concerns. Together with previous results, this supports use of this closed-loop system throughout pregnancy, labor, and the early postpartum period.
title: Intrapartum and Early Postpartum Use of Automated Insulin Delivery in Type 1 Diabetes: A Prespecified Analysis of the CIRCUIT Randomized Controlled Trial.

text: The Burden of Stigma in Type 2 Diabetes: Evidence from a Rural Primary Care Sample in Türkiye.. This study aimed to evaluate the presence of diabetes-related stigma and its relationship with disease control and family functioning among adults with type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) living in rural Türkiye
title: The Burden of Stigma in Type 2 Diabetes: Evidence from a Rural Primary Care Sample in Türkiye.

text: . A cross-sectional study was conducted between March and May 2025 at a Family Health Center (FHC). A total of 201 adults with physician-diagnosed T2DM participated in the study. Data were collected through face-to-face interviews using a sociodemographic questionnaire, the Diabetes Stigma Assessment Scale-2 (DSAS-2), and the Family APGAR scale, which assesses family functioning
title: The Burden of Stigma in Type 2 Diabetes: Evidence from a Rural Primary Care Sample in Türkiye.

text: . Statistical analyses included correlation tests, group comparisons, and logistic regression to identify independent predictors of stigma. The mean total DSAS-2 score was 39.4±9.2, indicating a moderate level of perceived stigma. Higher stigma scores were associated with very low income, polypharmacy, and the presence of comorbid chronic diseases (p<0.05)
title: The Burden of Stigma in Type 2 Diabetes: Evidence from a Rural Primary Care Sample in Türkiye.

text: . A positive correlation was found between the number of children and both the "Treated Differently" and "Self-Stigma" subdimensions of the DSAS-2 (r=0.202 and r=0.216, respectively). Family APGAR scores were generally high (mean=8.9±2.0), but no significant association was observed between family functioning and stigma levels
title: The Burden of Stigma in Type 2 Diabetes: Evidence from a Rural Primary Care Sample in Türkiye.

text: . Logistic regression analysis showed that medication use was independently associated with higher stigma (OR: 2.48; 95% CI: 1.23-4.98; p=0.011), whereas moderate income was associated with lower stigma (OR: 0.165; 95% CI: 0.048-0.567; p=0.004). Diabetes-related stigma remains a notable psychosocial challenge for adults with T2DM in rural settings
title: The Burden of Stigma in Type 2 Diabetes: Evidence from a Rural Primary Care Sample in Türkiye.

text: . Socioeconomic disadvantage, comorbidity, and family burden contribute to the internalization of stigma, whereas family support alone may not mitigate its effects. Addressing stigma within primary care through culturally tailored psychoeducation and empowerment programs may enhance both emotional well-being and disease management in rural populations.
title: The Burden of Stigma in Type 2 Diabetes: Evidence from a Rural Primary Care Sample in Türkiye.

text: Reporting Gaps in mHealth Intervention Studies for Adults With Diabetes: Systematic Review.. Diabetes self-management education and support requires scalable digital solutions, making mobile health (mHealth) interventions increasingly vital
title: Reporting Gaps in mHealth Intervention Studies for Adults With Diabetes: Systematic Review.

text: . Despite their proven clinical efficacy, the real-world translation and scalability of these interventions are severely hindered by fragmented and opaque reporting. To address this methodological gap, the World Health Organization developed the mHealth evidence reporting and assessment (mERA) checklist to standardize reporting transparency
title: Reporting Gaps in mHealth Intervention Studies for Adults With Diabetes: Systematic Review.

text: . This study aimed to systematically evaluate the reporting completeness of published randomized controlled trials (RCTs) on mHealth interventions for adult diabetes using the mERA checklist; identify critical reporting gaps; analyze how these deficiencies undermine feasibility, scalability, and sustainability; and propose targeted strategies for future optimization
title: Reporting Gaps in mHealth Intervention Studies for Adults With Diabetes: Systematic Review.

text: . A PRISMA (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses)-compliant systematic review was conducted. Five major databases (PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, MEDLINE, and the Cochrane Library) were systematically searched for relevant RCTs published from inception to July 2026
title: Reporting Gaps in mHealth Intervention Studies for Adults With Diabetes: Systematic Review.

text: . Data extraction and reporting completeness assessments were conducted using the 16-item mERA core checklist. Nonparametric and categorical analyses were used to evaluate factors associated with reporting completeness. A total of 144 RCTs conducted across 49 countries were included in the final analysis. The mean overall mERA reporting score was 6.74 out of 16 (SD 2.71)
title: Reporting Gaps in mHealth Intervention Studies for Adults With Diabetes: Systematic Review.

text: . While basic characteristics such as intervention delivery (n=128, 88.9%) and technology platform (n=117, 81.3%) were well reported, critical system-level domains were largely omitted. Specifically, interoperability (n=12, 8.3%), data security (n=28, 19.4%), compliance with guidelines (n=41, 28.5%), and intervention fidelity (n=53, 36.8%) were severely underreported
title: Reporting Gaps in mHealth Intervention Studies for Adults With Diabetes: Systematic Review.

text: . Additionally, reporting completeness was significantly higher in studies published between 2016 and 2026 ( Empirical research on mHealth interventions for adult diabetes exhibits systemic structural flaws in reporting, particularly concerning system integration, data security, and regulatory compliance
title: Reporting Gaps in mHealth Intervention Studies for Adults With Diabetes: Systematic Review.

text: . These omissions significantly undermine the transparency, reproducibility, and real-world scalability of digital diabetes care solutions. Future trials must rigorously adopt standardized reporting frameworks such as the mERA checklist to bridge the gap between clinical efficacy and large-scale public health policy translation.
title: Reporting Gaps in mHealth Intervention Studies for Adults With Diabetes: Systematic Review.

text: Diabetes and skin health: a statewide survey on Ohio healthcare providers' knowledge.. With increasing rates of diabetes, there is an increased incidence of diabetes skin conditions, yet the extent to which healthcare professionals are aware of these skin conditions is unclear
title: Diabetes and skin health: a statewide survey on Ohio healthcare providers' knowledge.

text: . The purpose of this study was to assess Ohio healthcare providers' (HCPs) understanding of diabetes dermatological manifestations, which can serve as early indicators of diabetes and impact diabetes management
title: Diabetes and skin health: a statewide survey on Ohio healthcare providers' knowledge.

text: . An online survey was distributed from February 2025 to March 2025 to collect data on demographics, frequency of dermatological issues in practice, screening practices, self-efficacy, knowledge of diabetes-related skin conditions, and preferences for further education, with 167 Ohio HCPs surveyed
title: Diabetes and skin health: a statewide survey on Ohio healthcare providers' knowledge.

text: . Survey distribution included mass e-mails sent through the Clinical and Translational Research Unit (CTRU) by University Communications and Marketing (UCM) at Ohio University, individual e-mails to Ohio professional societies for physician assistants and nurse practitioners, and posts on social media. Importantly, 66.5% of participants were early career HCPs with 10 years or less of experience
title: Diabetes and skin health: a statewide survey on Ohio healthcare providers' knowledge.

text: . Participants were nurse practitioners (28.7%), physician assistants (15.6%), resident physicians (26.3%), and attending physicians (29.3%). Regarding diabetes technology, 61.1% of the sample stated they rarely encountered patients with skin reactions from diabetes technology
title: Diabetes and skin health: a statewide survey on Ohio healthcare providers' knowledge.

text: . Notably, over half of respondents (56.3%) received a score of 50% or less on the dermatology and diabetes knowledge test and only 41.9% of respondents reported moderate confidence in diagnosing diabetes dermatologic manifestations. These findings suggest potential knowledge gaps on the topic, which warrants further evaluation of the quality of diabetes care and patient outcomes
title: Diabetes and skin health: a statewide survey on Ohio healthcare providers' knowledge.

text: . These results may help inform educational efforts for HCPs to enhance overall knowledge of dermatologic manifestations of diabetes. Further studies should assess knowledge and practice patterns among primary care healthcare professionals.
title: Diabetes and skin health: a statewide survey on Ohio healthcare providers' knowledge.

text: Blood Glucose Management Behaviour Among Haemodialysis Patients with Diabetes: A Qualitative Study Guided by the Theory of Planned Behaviour.
title: Blood Glucose Management Behaviour Among Haemodialysis Patients with Diabetes: A Qualitative Study Guided by the Theory of Planned Behaviour.

text: . To utilise the Theory of Planned Behaviour as a theoretical framework, employing qualitative interviews to gain an in-depth understanding and analysis of the motivations and influencing factors of blood glucose management behaviours among haemodialysis patients with diabetes
title: Blood Glucose Management Behaviour Among Haemodialysis Patients with Diabetes: A Qualitative Study Guided by the Theory of Planned Behaviour.

text: . Employing the phenomenological research method within qualitative research, in-depth semi-structured interviews were conducted with 12 haemodialysis patients with diabetes. Themes were then categorised using Colaizzi's seven-step content analysis method. Themes were categorised according to the Theory of Planned Behaviour, yielding four categories: 1
title: Blood Glucose Management Behaviour Among Haemodialysis Patients with Diabetes: A Qualitative Study Guided by the Theory of Planned Behaviour.

text: . Attitudes towards blood glucose management: perceived benefits and perceived burdens; 2. Subjective norms for blood glucose management: injunctive norms and descriptive norms; 3. Perceived behavioural control for blood glucose management: facilitating factors and impeding factors; 4
title: Blood Glucose Management Behaviour Among Haemodialysis Patients with Diabetes: A Qualitative Study Guided by the Theory of Planned Behaviour.

text: . Behavioural intention versus actual behaviour: high intention-high execution, high intention-low execution, low intention-low execution, comprising nine themes in total
title: Blood Glucose Management Behaviour Among Haemodialysis Patients with Diabetes: A Qualitative Study Guided by the Theory of Planned Behaviour.

text: . Using the Theory of Planned Behaviour, this study identifies key modifiable factors underlying glycaemic self-management among diabetic patients on maintenance haemodialysis, including conflicting attitudes, social-norm influences, and major perceived-behavioural-control barriers that produce intention-behaviour gaps
title: Blood Glucose Management Behaviour Among Haemodialysis Patients with Diabetes: A Qualitative Study Guided by the Theory of Planned Behaviour.

text: . Interventions should shift from knowledge-only education towards enhancing patients' practical execution and perceived control. Individualised feasible management plans, together with integrated support from healthcare teams, families and social resources, are needed to address real-world barriers and improve glycaemic self-management outcomes for this patient group.
title: Blood Glucose Management Behaviour Among Haemodialysis Patients with Diabetes: A Qualitative Study Guided by the Theory of Planned Behaviour.

text: Physical and Psychological Health in Adolescents and Young Adults With Type 1 Diabetes: The Mediating Roles of Diabetes Self-Management and Social Relationships.
title: Physical and Psychological Health in Adolescents and Young Adults With Type 1 Diabetes: The Mediating Roles of Diabetes Self-Management and Social Relationships.
journal: The science of diabetes self-management and care

text: . The purpose of this study was to examine whether diabetes self-management and social relationships mediate the association between self-perceived physical health and psychological health among Israeli adolescents and young adults with type 1 diabetes (T1D)
title: Physical and Psychological Health in Adolescents and Young Adults With Type 1 Diabetes: The Mediating Roles of Diabetes Self-Management and Social Relationships.
journal: The science of diabetes self-management and care

text: . A cross-sectional online survey was conducted among 79 individuals ages 16 to 25 years with T1D, recruited through diabetes-related social media platforms. Participants completed self-report measures of diabetes self-management and quality of life
title: Physical and Psychological Health in Adolescents and Young Adults With Type 1 Diabetes: The Mediating Roles of Diabetes Self-Management and Social Relationships.
journal: The science of diabetes self-management and care

text: . Physical health, psychological health, and social relationships were assessed using the World Health Organization Quality of Life Questionnaire-Brief Version, and diabetes self-management was assessed using the Diabetes Self-Management Questionnaire. Parallel mediation analyses were conducted using PROCESS Model 4 with 5000 bootstrap resamples
title: Physical and Psychological Health in Adolescents and Young Adults With Type 1 Diabetes: The Mediating Roles of Diabetes Self-Management and Social Relationships.
journal: The science of diabetes self-management and care

text: . Better physical health was significantly associated with better psychological health. When diabetes self-management and social relationships were included in the model, the direct association remained significant. Significant indirect effects were found through social relationships and diabetes self-management
title: Physical and Psychological Health in Adolescents and Young Adults With Type 1 Diabetes: The Mediating Roles of Diabetes Self-Management and Social Relationships.
journal: The science of diabetes self-management and care

text: . The total indirect effect was significant, but the contrast between the 2 indirect effects was not. Diabetes self-management and social relationships statistically accounted for part of the association between physical and psychological health among adolescents and young adults with T1D
title: Physical and Psychological Health in Adolescents and Young Adults With Type 1 Diabetes: The Mediating Roles of Diabetes Self-Management and Social Relationships.
journal: The science of diabetes self-management and care

text: . Because the study was cross-sectional, the results should be interpreted as indirect associations rather than causal pathways. Overall, these findings highlight the importance of addressing both behavioral and interpersonal resources in diabetes care and education during the transition to adulthood.
title: Physical and Psychological Health in Adolescents and Young Adults With Type 1 Diabetes: The Mediating Roles of Diabetes Self-Management and Social Relationships.
journal: The science of diabetes self-management and care

text: Feasibility of the Comprehensive Overweight/Obesity Management Pre-Kidney Transplant Program: A Group-Based Lifestyle Intervention and GLP-1 Receptor Agonist Therapy for End-Stage Kidney Disease Candidates Ineligible Due to Obesity.
title: Feasibility of the Comprehensive Overweight/Obesity Management Pre-Kidney Transplant Program: A Group-Based Lifestyle Intervention and GLP-1 Receptor Agonist Therapy for End-Stage Kidney Disease Candidates Ineligible Due to Obesity.
journal: The science of diabetes self-management and care

text: . The purpose of this study was to evaluate the feasibility of applying a structured interprofessional weight-loss intervention to improve transplant eligibility among candidates with body mass index (BMI) >35 kg/m². The Comprehensive Overweight/Obesity Management Pre-Kidney Transplant (COMPKT) program was a single-arm feasibility study at an academic center
title: Feasibility of the Comprehensive Overweight/Obesity Management Pre-Kidney Transplant Program: A Group-Based Lifestyle Intervention and GLP-1 Receptor Agonist Therapy for End-Stage Kidney Disease Candidates Ineligible Due to Obesity.
journal: The science of diabetes self-management and care

text: . Participants attended 15 weekly virtual group education sessions using the National Diabetes Prevention Program PreventT2 curriculum delivered by trained lifestyle coaches, with remote monitoring and interprofessional pharmacotherapy management including glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptor agonist or GLP-1/glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide co-agonist therapy when clinically
title: Feasibility of the Comprehensive Overweight/Obesity Management Pre-Kidney Transplant Program: A Group-Based Lifestyle Intervention and GLP-1 Receptor Agonist Therapy for End-Stage Kidney Disease Candidates Ineligible Due to Obesity.
journal: The science of diabetes self-management and care

text: polypeptide co-agonist therapy when clinically appropriate
title: Feasibility of the Comprehensive Overweight/Obesity Management Pre-Kidney Transplant Program: A Group-Based Lifestyle Intervention and GLP-1 Receptor Agonist Therapy for End-Stage Kidney Disease Candidates Ineligible Due to Obesity.
journal: The science of diabetes self-management and care

text: . Feasibility outcomes were enrollment, attendance, and GLP-1 uptake; clinical outcomes were BMI and percentage weight change. Twenty-nine participants from the first 3 cohorts (median baseline BMI 41.1 kg/m²; interquartile range 40.4-44.8) were analyzed. Attendance varied: 44.8% attended < 50% of sessions, 20.7% attended 50% to 75%, and 34.5% attended > 75%
title: Feasibility of the Comprehensive Overweight/Obesity Management Pre-Kidney Transplant Program: A Group-Based Lifestyle Intervention and GLP-1 Receptor Agonist Therapy for End-Stage Kidney Disease Candidates Ineligible Due to Obesity.
journal: The science of diabetes self-management and care

text: . GLP-1 therapy use rose from 62.1% at baseline to 72.4% at session 15, with 52.4% reaching high-dose therapy. Median weight change was -3.44% (range -10.89% to +1.91%). Participants attending ≥ 50% of sessions had greater median weight loss than those with lower attendance, independent of GLP-1 use. Two participants received kidney transplants during the evaluation period
title: Feasibility of the Comprehensive Overweight/Obesity Management Pre-Kidney Transplant Program: A Group-Based Lifestyle Intervention and GLP-1 Receptor Agonist Therapy for End-Stage Kidney Disease Candidates Ineligible Due to Obesity.
journal: The science of diabetes self-management and care

text: . COMPKT was feasible and produced modest but clinically meaningful weight loss in a high-risk population. Session engagement, rather than GLP-1 pharmacotherapy alone, appeared to drive outcomes, informing future program design and implementation.
title: Feasibility of the Comprehensive Overweight/Obesity Management Pre-Kidney Transplant Program: A Group-Based Lifestyle Intervention and GLP-1 Receptor Agonist Therapy for End-Stage Kidney Disease Candidates Ineligible Due to Obesity.
